ThaiCERT 2026-04-02 + CERT/CC VU#221883 demonstrate that an untrusted prompt walks the chain to host RCE without further exploitation.
rules.limitations: Fires only when all four shapes (an unsafe-mode `CodeInterpreterTool`, a `JSONSearchTool` or `JSONLoader` path, a `RagTool` or `WebsiteSearchTool` URL, and a missing Docker check) are found in one file. The same shapes split across two modules are never reported as the chain, and a comment that mentions `assert_codeinterp_safe_mode(` removes one shape from the count. A Python file over 512 KB is not read.
rules.remediation: Apply each child-rule's remediation. The single hardest gate is CVE-2026-2275 (CodeInterpreterTool unsafe_mode); fixing that one breaks the chain. The runtime helpers in `agent_audit_kit.sanitizers.crewai` collectively suppress all four sub-rules.
rules.title: CrewAI four-CVE exploit chain reachable in one module

rules.description: `CodeInterpreterTool(unsafe_mode=True)` drops into a host Python interpreter where ctypes / os.system are reachable. CVE-2026-2275 is the canonical sandbox-escape primitive in the CrewAI 0.x chain (ThaiCERT 2026-04-02 / CERT/CC VU#221883; CWE-749, CVSS 9.6 CRITICAL per NVD — the Docker-unreachable fallback to SandboxPython enables RCE via arbitrary C function calling).
rules.limitations: Fires on a literal `unsafe_mode=True` in a `CodeInterpreterTool(...)` call in a file that imports crewai. `unsafe_mode` taken from a variable or a setting is not read, and the guard is looked for as text in the enclosing function, so a comment that mentions `assert_codeinterp_safe_mode(` silences it. A Python file over 512 KB is not read.
rules.remediation: Set `unsafe_mode=False` on every CodeInterpreterTool invocation. If you must run untrusted code, wrap with a real container sandbox and call `agent_audit_kit.sanitizers.crewai.assert_codeinterp_safe_mode(False)` in the same function to suppress this rule.
rules.title: CrewAI CodeInterpreterTool with unsafe_mode=True

rules.description: `JSONSearchTool(file_path=...)` / `JSONLoader(path=...)` accepts an attacker-influenceable path without anchoring to a project root. CVE-2026-2285 (arbitrary local file read, CVSS 7.5 HIGH per NVD): untrusted JSON-loader path lets the agent read arbitrary files (chained with the other three CVEs into host RCE).
rules.limitations: Needs a non-constant path argument and, in the same function, one of a short list of source spellings (`request.json`, `request.args`, `request.form`, `event`, `user_input`, `agent.kickoff(`, ...). `request.get_json()`, or a path that arrives as a function parameter, is not a source, so the call is not reported. A Python file over 512 KB is not read.
rules.remediation: Anchor every JSON-loader path with `agent_audit_kit.sanitizers.crewai.validate_jsonloader_path(path, root=...)` before passing into the tool. Calling the validator in the same function suppresses this rule.
rules.title: CrewAI JSON loader path traversal

rules.description: `RagTool(url=...)` / `WebsiteSearchTool(url=...)` accepts a non-constant URL reachable from an untrusted source without an allow-list / private-network guard. CVE-2026-2286 (CWE-918, CVSS 9.8 CRITICAL per NVD): cloud-metadata or loopback SSRF feeds back into the agent tool-use loop.
rules.limitations: Fires on `RagTool` or `WebsiteSearchTool` built with a non-constant `url`, `website` or `web_url` (or first positional argument) inside a function whose text contains `request.json`, `request.body`, `request.args`, `request.form`, `request.data`, `request.values`, `request.files`, `event`, `llm_input`, `user_input`, `agent.kickoff(`, `task.execute(` or `inputs=`, and no `validate_rag_url(` call. A URL that arrives as an ordinary function parameter (`def search(website_url)`) carries no marker and is not reported. `validate_rag_url` itself refuses a URL whose host Node, requests and Rust's `url` crate read differently from curl, httpx and urlsplit, which keep a backslash inside the authority. It resolves the host to check its addresses and the RAG tool resolves it again to fetch, so a name whose DNS answer changes in between (DNS rebinding) passes the check and is fetched at a private address. A Python file over 512 KB is not read.
rules.remediation: Wrap every RAG / website URL with `agent_audit_kit.sanitizers.crewai.validate_rag_url(url, allowlist=[...])`. The helper rejects private IPs after DNS resolution and enforces an explicit hostname allow-list.
rules.title: CrewAI RagTool / WebsiteSearchTool SSRF

rules.description: `CodeInterpreterTool(...)` does not gate execution on a Docker liveness check (`docker_required=True` is unset and `require_docker_liveness(client)` is not called). A dead Docker daemon silently falls back to the host Python interpreter, completing the chain to host RCE (CVE-2026-2287, CWE-94, CVSS 9.8 CRITICAL per NVD).
rules.limitations: Fires on every `CodeInterpreterTool(...)` call that has no literal `docker_required=True` and no `require_docker_liveness(` in the enclosing function. That text is matched as source, so a comment that mentions `require_docker_liveness(` silences it. A Python file over 512 KB is not read.
rules.remediation: Either set `docker_required=True` on CodeInterpreterTool or call `agent_audit_kit.sanitizers.crewai.require_docker_liveness(client)` in the same function — the helper raises before the tool ever sees the host fallback.
rules.title: CrewAI sandbox fallback without Docker liveness check

rules.description: A function that targets DeepSeek V4 (OpenAI-compatible client with `base_url=` containing 'deepseek', or `import deepseek`) reads from an untrusted source (request body, document loader, file read) and passes the value into a `tools=[{description: ...}]` payload without calling `sanitize_tool_description`. DeepSeek V4 (Apache 2.0, 2026-04-24) exposes MoE routing via its tool-call envelope — untrusted text inside a tool description can poison expert selection (LLM01 with MoE-specific surface). Speculative shape until corpus refresh.
rules.limitations: Python only, per function. A DeepSeek target is recognised only from a string literal containing `deepseek` in `base_url=`, or a `deepseek` import: a URL held in a constant is not seen. An untrusted source is recognised only from a short list (`request.json`, `request.args`, `pdfplumber.open`, `unstructured.partition`, `open(...).read()`), so a page fetched with `requests.get(url).text` is not one. A call to `sanitize_tool_description` counts anywhere in the function, whichever value it cleans. A substitution (`re.sub`, `re.subn`, or `.sub` or `.subn` on a compiled pattern, held by a name or compiled in place) counts only when its pattern is a string literal, or a name bound to one (by an assignment in the function, in a function around it or in the module, a module-level block included, directly or through `re.compile`), that names `route` or `expert` (in any case), the words in the routing tokens `[ROUTE: ...]`, `<|route_id|>`, `__route__=` and `{{expert: ...}}`, and its result is a description built in the same function (a `"description"` dict value, a `description=` keyword or a `["description"]` assignment) or is assigned to the variable a name in one stands for: by `=`, `+=` or `:=`, or as the first name a `subn(...)` unpacks into (`clean, n = re.subn(...)`). The substitution counts anywhere inside that value, so `doc + re.sub(ROUTE, "", suffix)` clears the function although `doc` goes out raw. A name, a pattern's included, is the variable Python resolves it to: that of the nearest function, this one or one around it, that binds it (a parameter, an assignment, an import), which a function nested in that one can also assign through `nonlocal`; a name a class body, a comprehension or a lambda inside the function binds counts as the function's own. The function is judged as a whole, the functions nested in it included, so one of them that cleans its description clears it too; a nested function is also judged on its own. One cleaned description clears a function, even when another tool's description goes out raw, the cleaned name is rebound to the raw text, or the keyword belongs to something else (`argparse.ArgumentParser(description=re.sub(...))`). What the pattern removes is not checked, so `re.sub(r"route", "path", doc)` counts, and a pattern built at run time or held on a class never does. A file over 512 KB is not read.
rules.remediation: Pipe untrusted tool descriptions through `agent_audit_kit.sanitizers.deepseek.sanitize_tool_description` before assembling the `tools=` payload. The sanitiser strips ANSI / control characters and routing-poison tokens ([ROUTE: ...], <|route_id|>, __route__=, etc.) and truncates to a max length. Calling it in the same function suppresses this rule.
rules.title: DeepSeek V4 MoE-routed tool description injection

rules.description: The upstream MCP Python, Java, Apollo and TypeScript SDKs shipped a StreamableHTTP transport that trusts the browser-supplied `Host` header. A malicious web page that a user visits can resolve a custom domain to 127.0.0.1 via DNS rebinding and reach a local MCP server, turning every browser tab into a remote-attack surface for stdio-grade tools. The upstream patch adds a Host allow-list; downstream servers embedding StreamableHTTP must enforce one too. See CVE-2025-66414 / CVE-2025-66416 (Python), CVE-2026-35568 (Java), CVE-2026-35577 (Apollo), CVE-2026-81102 (Python FastMCP), and CVE-2026-77363, a downstream server (obsidian-tc before 1.3.1) whose TypeScript transport checked neither Host nor Origin. Detection reads the raw SDK transport classes and, since v0.3.93, the Python **FastMCP** wrapper when it is told to run over a network transport (`run(transport="streamable-http"/"sse")`, `streamable_http_app()`, `sse_app()`). **stdio FastMCP servers are deliberately not flagged**: FastMCP defaults to stdio and a stdio server has no listener to rebind onto. **Binding to loopback is not a mitigation** and does not clear this rule -- CVE-2026-81102 was loopback-bound; the Host allow-list is the control. Single-file pattern detection with a project-wide mitigation check: one allow-list anywhere in the tree clears every candidate, so a server whose middleware lives in a separate package that is not scanned together will read as mitigated.
rules.limitations: A candidate is a .py, .ts, .tsx, .js, .mjs or .cjs file that builds a StreamableHTTP transport, or a Python FastMCP server run over a network transport. One Host allow-list anywhere in the project clears every candidate, whatever it protects: a Django `ALLOWED_HOSTS` in an unrelated app counts. A manifest over 2 MB, or a source file over 512 KB, is not read.
rules.remediation: Wrap the StreamableHTTP app with a Host-header allow-list. In Starlette / FastAPI attach `TrustedHostMiddleware(allowed_hosts=...)`; in Node attach an `allowedHosts:` option or a Host middleware; in Java/Apollo enable `HostHeaderFilter` / `allowedHosts` config. In Python FastMCP pass `transport_security=TransportSecuritySettings(allowed_hosts=[...])` when constructing the server, or run it over stdio. Alternatively upgrade the SDK to a patched version and pass through its host-validation option.
rules.title: MCP StreamableHTTP transport without Host-header allow-list

rules.description: A project dependency manifest (requirements.txt, pyproject.toml, package.json, pom.xml, build.gradle) pins an MCP SDK at a version below the DNS-rebinding fix, or declares a range that admits one. Patched versions: Python `mcp` >= 1.23.0, TS `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` >= 1.21.1, Java `io.modelcontextprotocol.sdk:mcp-core` >= 0.11.0, `@apollo/mcp-server` >= 1.7.0. Even if the project never serves over StreamableHTTP itself, transitive servers built on the SDK inherit the bug.
rules.limitations: Reads `mcp` in the root requirements*.txt and pyproject.toml, and `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` and `@apollo/mcp-server` in the root package.json, taking the lowest version a range allows, so a lower bound below the fix (`mcp>=1.2.0`) is reported. A git reference, a tarball (at a URL or behind `file:`) and a `workspace:` spec are judged by the release their tag, file name or range names (`github:o/r#v1.20.0`, `sdk-1.20.0.tgz`, `workspace:^1.20.0`), with releases compared on their first three numbers, so a pre-release of the fix (`#v1.21.1-rc.1`) reads as the fix. A declaration that states no version (`"latest"`, `workspace:*`, a `file:` directory, a git reference to a commit or a branch, which is any name holding a `/` but `refs/tags/<tag>`) is not reported. `io.modelcontextprotocol.sdk:mcp-core` below 0.11.0 is read as written in the root pom.xml and Gradle files. Declarations of one install that no release satisfies together (`mcp==1.23.0` beside `mcp==1.22.0` in one requirements file) admit nothing and are not reported; pip refuses to install them too. A lockfile (uv.lock, package-lock.json), a pyproject.toml that does not parse, and a manifest in a sub-directory or over 2 MB are not read. A source file over 512 KB is not read. A pyproject.toml with a key of more than 64 dotted parts, or holding an integer Python cannot convert (one past 4,300 digits), is refused and reported as AAK-INTERNAL-SCANNER-FAIL.
rules.remediation: Bump the SDK to the patched version listed in the rule title. If a bump is not yet possible, ensure every transport surface has its own Host-header allow-list (see AAK-DNS-REBIND-001 remediation).
rules.title: Vulnerable MCP SDK version pinned (DNS-rebinding fix missing)

rules.description: Two-arm detector for the OX MCP 2026-05-01 disclosure batch. Arm 1 — pin-check on the npm `docsgpt` / `docsgpt-mcp` package, GitHub `arc53/DocsGPT` git refs in package.json / lockfiles, and the same package in `pyproject.toml` / `requirements*.txt`. Fires for any pin below the patched 0.6.4 floor. Arm 2 — server-config scanner that fires when a DocsGPT MCP config declares a safe transport (`sse` / `http` / `https`) but permits a post-handshake `transport=stdio` override (the MITM transport-flip path the disclosure traced through CVE-2026-26015). The architectural receiver-side class is already covered by AAK-MCP-STDIO-CMD-INJ-001/002/003/004 + AAK-STDIO-001 (shipped v0.3.6); this rule adds the product-named pin row consumers expect when grepping CHANGELOG.cves.md for 'DocsGPT' plus the transport-flip-resistance check the receiver-side rules don't catch.
rules.limitations: Two arms. The pin reads npm `docsgpt` and `docsgpt-mcp` in the root package.json, package-lock.json, yarn.lock and pnpm-lock.yaml, and the name followed directly by a version in the root requirements*.txt and pyproject.toml, and reports a version below 0.6.4 or any `arc53/DocsGPT` git reference. A `node_modules/docsgpt` entry that only a transitive dependency adds to package-lock.json, a version recorded only in uv.lock (name and version sit on separate lines), a sub-directory package.json and an `arc53/docsgpt` image tag in a compose file are not read. The config arm reads JSON MCP configs (.mcp.json, mcp.json, `.cursor/mcp.json`, `.vscode/mcp.json`), DocsGPT's own config files at the root and in `.docsgpt/`, and the .json files of a top-level `configs/`, and reports one that names DocsGPT, declares an sse, http, https or streamable-http transport and enables stdio explicitly (`stdio_fallback`, `transport_override`, `permit_transport_override` or a `transports` list that includes stdio); the same settings in `deploy/docsgpt.config.json` are not reported. A config file over 1 MB, a manifest over 2 MB, or a lockfile over 32 MiB, is not read.
rules.remediation: Pin DocsGPT >= 0.6.4 (the vendor fix from the OX 2026-05-01 batch). That version pin is the control that actually works today. For the transport-flip path itself, protect the channel rather than the config: serve the MCP endpoint over TLS with certificate verification enabled so a middlebox cannot rewrite the handshake, and prefer a client that pins the transport it negotiated. The receiver-side detectors (AAK-MCP-STDIO-CMD-INJ-*, AAK-STDIO-001) catch the downstream command injection if a flip does succeed. **Note on `deny_stdio_transport` / `allowed_transports`:** this rule treats those keys as a short-circuit, but they are AgentAuditKit conventions, not fields the MCP specification defines — they appear in none of the 748 public MCP configs in this project's corpus. Adding them silences this rule and is ignored by your MCP client, so do not treat their presence as protection.
rules.title: DocsGPT MCP transport-flip MITM (OX 2026-05-01, CVE-2026-26015 family)

rules.description: Project depends on `apache-doris-mcp-server` at a version < 0.6.1. CVE-2025-66335 is a query-context neutralization bypass in the MCP adapter's tool layer — crafted tool arguments are concatenated into Doris SQL without a parameterized boundary, letting an LLM-driven tool call reach into arbitrary reads/writes. CVE-2025-66336 is a sibling SQL injection in a metadata query path (a user-controlled database name interpolated without the caller's authz context), same < 0.6.1 fixed line. Fixed in 0.6.1.
rules.limitations: Reads the dependency declarations of the root requirements*.txt, pyproject.toml and Pipfile in their own formats, and reports one whose range admits a release below 0.6.1 (`apache-doris-mcp-server<0.6.1` included), and the version the root Pipfile.lock, poetry.lock or uv.lock resolves when it is below 0.6.1. A git requirement's dotted release tag is read as its version (`@v0.5.0`); a commit, a branch or a tag with no dot (`@v2`) states none. A declaration that states no version, such as `apache-doris-mcp-server` alone or a git URL without a release tag, is not reported, and neither is a requirements file in a sub-directory or an `.mcp.json` launcher. A manifest over 2 MB is not read. A lockfile over 32 MiB is not read.
rules.remediation: Upgrade `apache-doris-mcp-server` to 0.6.1 or newer. Audit every tool the adapter exposes to confirm arguments flow through a parameterized query builder, never string concatenation.
rules.title: apache-doris-mcp-server < 0.6.1 SQL injection

rules.description: An agent config declares two or more locales (or `multilingual: true`) for a user-facing surface, but the repository's eval / test fixtures reference only a single language. Cross-lingual robustness is a required-evidence axis under EU AI Act Article 15 (binding for Annex III high-risk use cases on 2027-12-02 and for Annex I product-embedded high-risk systems on 2028-08-02), and Ford et al. 2026 (arXiv:2605.23157) document that single-language safety eval misses language-specific jailbreak / refusal-regression vectors that scale non-uniformly across languages.
rules.limitations: Counts a locale as evaluated when its code appears in the path of any file under a directory named `evals`, `fixtures`, `scenarios`, `i18n`, `locales`, `benchmarks` and the like, whatever the file holds, so `locales/fr.json`, a file of UI strings, counts as an eval for French. It recognises 30 two-letter language codes (`ta` and `te` are not among them) and finds agent configs by file name (`agent.yaml`, `crew.yaml`, `manifest.yaml` and a few more; `config.yaml` is not read). A config file over 1 MB is not read.
rules.remediation: Add per-locale eval fixtures matching the declared locale set (one scenario file per language, or a parametrized eval matrix), or narrow the agent config's declared locales to the set you can evidence. The EU AI Act Article 15 evidence pack must show robustness testing across each user-facing language.
rules.title: Multilingual user-facing agent lacks per-locale eval coverage

rules.description: Project depends on `excel-mcp-server` at a version <= 0.1.7. CVE-2026-40576 is a path-traversal in the server's `get_excel_path()` helper — absolute paths pass through unchecked, relative paths are joined without resolving-and-validating the result. Combined with the default 0.0.0.0 bind + zero authentication on SSE / Streamable-HTTP, any unauthenticated network peer can read, write or overwrite files anywhere on the host. Fixed in 0.1.8.
rules.limitations: Reads the dependency declarations of the root requirements*.txt, pyproject.toml and Pipfile in their own formats, and reports one whose range admits a release below 0.1.8 (`excel-mcp-server<0.1.8` included), and the version the root Pipfile.lock, poetry.lock or uv.lock resolves when it is below 0.1.8. A git requirement's dotted release tag is read as its version (`@v0.1.7`); a commit, a branch or a tag with no dot (`@v2`) states none. A declaration that states no version, such as `excel-mcp-server` alone or a git URL without a release tag, is not reported, and neither is a requirements file in a sub-directory or an `.mcp.json` launcher. A manifest over 2 MB is not read. A lockfile over 32 MiB is not read.
rules.remediation: Upgrade `excel-mcp-server` to 0.1.8 or later. Until the bump is in, bind the server to 127.0.0.1 and front it with an auth proxy.
rules.title: excel-mcp-server <= 0.1.7 path traversal

rules.description: Package manifest depends on `flowise` or `flowise-components` at version < 3.1.2, and/or a Flowise flow config (`.flowise/*.json`, `flows/*.json`) declares an MCP adapter node with `customFunction` or `runCode` sinks. The Custom-MCP feature is a recurring RCE class: CVE-2026-40933 (GHSA-c9gw-hvqq-f33r, CVSS 10.0) lets an authenticated attacker combine allowlisted commands like `npx` with execution flags such as `-c` for arbitrary OS command execution; CVE-2025-71336 (< 3.0.6, CVSS 9.8) is an unsandboxed RCE in the same feature; CVE-2026-56274 (< 3.1.2, CVSS 9.9) adds OS command injection via incomplete command-flag validation plus a regex bypass in local file-access restrictions; CVE-2026-58057 (< 3.1.3, CVSS 5.0) validates Custom-MCP stdio env vars against a *case-sensitive* denylist, so on Windows (case-insensitive env names) `node_options` slips past the NODE_OPTIONS entry and reaches `NODE_OPTIONS --require` code execution. CVE-2026-69263 (< 3.1.3, CVSS 8.7) is the same denylist-bypass class one step on: the denylist matched exact env-var names, but `npm_config_yes=true` reproduces `npx --yes` auto-install-and-execute without using a blocked flag; CVE-2026-69257 (< 3.1.3, CVSS 7.6) is a separate SSRF where `httpSecurity.ts` did not normalise IPv4-mapped IPv6 (`::ffff:127.0.0.1`), letting the MCP tool path reach loopback / cloud-metadata endpoints. Pin floor is 3.1.3 (highest fixed version) so 3.0.6–3.1.2 are still flagged. Same architectural class as Ox's original STDIO disclosure (see AAK-STDIO-001).
rules.limitations: The version arm reads `flowise` and `flowise-components` under `dependencies`, `devDependencies` and `peerDependencies` of the root package.json only, and reports a range that admits a version below 3.1.3, or a spec that states no version. package-lock.json, yarn.lock, pnpm-lock.yaml, `optionalDependencies`, `overrides`, a sub-directory package.json, an `npx flowise` launcher in .mcp.json and a `flowiseai/flowise` image tag in a compose file are not read. The flow arm reads `.flowise/*.json`, `flows/*.json` and `flows/**/*.json` that mention MCP and carry a `customFunction`, `runCode` or `executeCommand` key, so an export saved as `chatflows/export.json` is not reported. A package.json over 2 MB, or a flow file over 1 MB, is not read.
rules.remediation: Upgrade flowise and flowise-components to 3.1.3 or later. Audit every MCP adapter node in your flow configs; remove `customFunction`/`runCode` sinks unless they're validated against a strict argv allowlist, and treat env-var denylists as case-insensitive. See also AAK-STDIO-001 for the architectural-class detector.
rules.title: Flowise < 3.1.2 MCP adapter authenticated RCE

rules.description: A workflow in `.github/workflows/` uses a third-party Action (`owner/action@ref`) where `ref` is a tag or branch name instead of a 40-character commit SHA. A repo-takeover of the Action's publisher can re-point the tag to a malicious revision — the downstream repo consuming it will happily run the new code with `GITHUB_TOKEN` and write permissions. GitHub's April 2026 Security Roadmap ships Immutable Actions and makes SHA pinning the default policy.
rules.limitations: Reads the `uses:` entries of the files directly inside `.github/workflows` and reports an `owner/action@ref` whose ref is not a 40-character commit SHA, except for the owners `actions` and `github`, local `./` actions and `docker://` images. A third-party action referenced from a local composite action (`.github/actions/setup/action.yml`) is not read, and neither is an `actions/` or `github/` action pinned to a branch (`actions/checkout@main`) or a `docker://` image tag. A workflow file over 1 MB is not read.
rules.remediation: Repin third-party Actions to a 40-character commit SHA and add a `# v1.2.3`-style trailing comment for humans. First-party Actions under `actions/` and `github/` are exempt (they now ship Immutable Actions). Dependabot will auto-bump SHA pins when `update-type: all` is set.
rules.title: Third-party GitHub Action not pinned by full commit SHA

rules.description: A `run:` step in a GitHub Actions workflow expands the secrets context (`toJSON(secrets)`, `secrets.X`, or an env var set from a secret) or the whole environment (`env`, `printenv`, `set`) and passes it through an encoder or transformer (base32, base64, xxd, od, rev, gzip, `openssl enc` and the like) whose output reaches the job log. GitHub masks a secret in the log only where its exact value appears, so an encoded copy prints in full, and anyone who can read the log can decode it. The Gheist campaign (Wiz, 2026-10-25) pushed exactly this step, `echo -n '${{ toJSON(secrets) }}' | base32 -w 120`, on `ci-sync-*` branches of every repository stolen tokens could reach, then downloaded the log and deleted the run.
rules.limitations: Reads the `run:` steps of the workflow files directly inside `.github/workflows`; a composite action, a reusable workflow kept elsewhere and the code of an action are not read. A command line is joined across backslash continuations, split at `;`, `&&` and `||`, and its pipeline at `|`; secret material reaches an encoder through a pipe, a here-string, a heredoc or a process substitution. Secret material is a `secrets` expression (`toJSON(secrets)`, `secrets.X`, `secrets['X']`), an env var that a workflow, job or step `env:` sets from one, or a whole-environment dump (`env` without a command, `printenv`, `set` without arguments, `export -p`, `declare -p` or `-x`). A step is reported only when the encoded output reaches the log: the pipeline ends in a program that prints (an encoder, `cat`, `tee`, `tr`, `sed`, `jq` and the like) and redirects it nowhere but stdout, stderr or `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY`. A secret written to a file, to `$GITHUB_OUTPUT` or `$GITHUB_ENV`, or piped into a program that consumes it (`docker login --password-stdin`, `gpg --import`) is not reported, and neither is a dump made by a script the step calls or through a variable the step builds. CRITICAL when the workflow carries a published Gheist marker: the file `sync-check.yml` with the step `toJSON(secrets) }}' | base32 -w 120`, or the string `===== gdmp-pivot:`. A workflow file over 1 MB is not read.
rules.remediation: Remove the step. If you did not write it, treat every repository, organization and environment secret the workflow could read as exposed: rotate them, revoke the token that pushed the commit, and look for `ci-sync-*` branches and for workflow runs deleted soon after they finished (`workflows.delete_workflow_run` in the audit log). To give a tool a secret, pass it as an env var or on stdin; never print it, encoded or not.
rules.title: Workflow step prints secrets through an encoder

rules.description: Phase 2 sibling of AAK-DOCSGPT-MCP-STDIO-MITM-001 (v0.3.14). Two-arm detector for assafelovic/gpt-researcher under the OX MCP 2026-05-01 disclosure batch. Arm 1 — pin-check on the PyPI `gpt-researcher` / `gpt-researcher-mcp` packages (primary surface), plus npm + GitHub `assafelovic/gpt-researcher` git refs. Latest PyPI release is 0.14.8 (2026-03-13), pre-disclosure — vendor has not shipped a post-disclosure fix as of the AAK ship date, so the rule fires for any pinned version (same `patched_in: None` posture as astro-mcp / chatgpt-mcp). Arm 2 — server-config scanner `gpt_researcher_transport_flip.py` that fires when a GPT-Researcher-named MCP config declares an SSE/HTTP transport but permits a post-handshake `transport=stdio` override (the MITM transport-flip path). Configs that explicitly set `deny_stdio_transport: true` or `allowed_transports: ["sse"]` short-circuit the rule. Architectural receiver-side class is covered by AAK-MCP-STDIO-CMD-INJ-001 (Python).
rules.limitations: Two arms. The pin reads `gpt-researcher` and `gpt-researcher-mcp` followed directly by a version in the root requirements*.txt and pyproject.toml, and in the root npm manifests, and reports every version because no fix exists. A name with no version, a requirements file in a sub-directory, a version recorded only in uv.lock (name and version sit on separate lines) and a `gptresearcher/gpt-researcher` image tag in a compose file are not reported. The config arm reads JSON MCP configs (.mcp.json, mcp.json, `.cursor/mcp.json`, `.vscode/mcp.json`), gpt-researcher's own config files at the root and in `.gpt-researcher/`, and the .json files of a top-level `configs/`, and reports one that names gpt-researcher, declares an sse, http, https or streamable-http transport and enables stdio explicitly (`stdio_fallback`, `transport_override`, `permit_transport_override` or a `transports` list that includes stdio); the same settings in `deploy/gpt-researcher.config.json` are not reported. A config file over 1 MB, a manifest over 2 MB, or a lockfile over 32 MiB, is not read.
rules.remediation: Pin `gpt-researcher` away from any pre-disclosure version when the vendor ships a post-2026-05-01 fix (track at https://github.com/assafelovic/gpt-researcher). That version pin is the control that actually works today. For the transport-flip path itself, protect the channel rather than the config: serve the MCP endpoint over TLS with certificate verification enabled so a middlebox cannot rewrite the handshake, and prefer a client that pins the transport it negotiated. **Note on `deny_stdio_transport` / `allowed_transports`:** this rule treats those keys as a short-circuit, but they are AgentAuditKit conventions, not fields the MCP specification defines — they appear in none of the 748 public MCP configs in this project's corpus. Adding them silences this rule and is ignored by your MCP client, so do not treat their presence as protection.
rules.title: GPT-Researcher MCP transport-flip MITM (OX 2026-05-01, CVE-2025-65720)

rules.description: A tool description, SKILL.md body, agent card, or system prompt represents the AI as a therapist / counselor / psychologist / 'qualified mental health professional'. Tennessee SB 1580 (signed 2026-04-01) makes this unlawful and enforceable via the TN Consumer Protection Act, with a **private right of action** and $5,000 civil penalty per violation.
rules.limitations: Reads `.md`, `.json`, `.yaml`, `.yml` and `.txt` files and matches a short phrase list: `I am a/your therapist`, `act as a/your counselor`, `provide therapy`, `deliver psychotherapy`, `replace your therapist` (or replaces, replaced, replacing) and `licensed mental health professional`, passing over one with not, never, no, cannot or n't (its apostrophe straight, curly or U+02BC, or left out of a common contraction such as `isnt`) among the four words before it, within 200 characters, on its line and in its clause, or with `without`, `instead of` or `rather than` directly before it (`no human`, `no clinician`, `no physician`, `no doctor` and `not only` never count). The contraction `I'm your therapist`, `acts as` and `acting as your counselor`, `provides` and `providing therapy`, and `delivers` and `delivering psychotherapy` are not matched: on 632 healthcare READMEs and docs from GitHub code search, 24 of the 459 findings they added were an AI's claim. A claim in the second person (`You are a licensed therapist`), one with a negation of something else among those four words (`If you are not in crisis, I am your therapist`) and a persona written in a `.py` file are not matched either.
rules.remediation: Rewrite the description. The AI can support mental-wellness use cases but cannot claim or imply it is (or replaces) a licensed mental-health professional. Add an explicit 'not a substitute for licensed care' disclaimer.
rules.title: AI described as a mental-health professional (Tennessee SB 1580)

rules.description: A prompt, tool description, SKILL.md body or agent card in a Markdown, JSON, YAML or text file describes an AI system making prior-authorization or medical-necessity decisions without licensed-physician review. Kansas, Washington, and Utah 2026 laws require a clinician in the loop for these decisions.
rules.limitations: Reads `.md`, `.json`, `.yaml`, `.yml` and `.txt` files and matches an adverb or a `no human` phrase, a verb in its base form and a singular decision object, as in `automatically approve prior authorization`, passing over one with not, never, no, cannot or n't (its apostrophe straight, curly or U+02BC, or left out of a common contraction such as `isnt`) among the four words before it, within 200 characters, on its line and in its clause, or with `without`, `instead of` or `rather than` directly before it (`no human`, `no clinician`, `no physician`, `no doctor` and `not only` never count). The third person, the -ing form and a plural object (`automatically approves prior authorization requests`, `automatically deny claims`) are not matched: on 632 healthcare READMEs and docs from GitHub code search, none of the 15 findings they added was an AI deciding medical necessity. A prefixed verb (`auto-denies medical necessity appeals`), a missing review stated after the object (`with no physician review`), a decision with a negation of something else among those four words (`If not reviewed, it will automatically approve ...`) and a rule written in a `.py` file are not matched either.
rules.remediation: Route every prior-auth / medical-necessity output through a licensed-physician review step; expose that review in the audit log.
rules.title: AI makes prior-authorization / medical-necessity decisions alone

rules.description: A prompt, tool description, SKILL.md body or agent card in a Markdown, JSON, YAML or text file describes an AI system approving or denying insurance coverage without a human in the loop. Georgia and Iowa 2026 laws restrict AI-only coverage / benefit determinations.
rules.limitations: Reads `.md`, `.json`, `.yaml`, `.yml` and `.txt` files and matches `AI`, `algorithm` or `model`, then `only`, `solely` or `alone`, a decision verb and an object, singular or plural, as in `AI solely denies claims`, passing over one with not, never, no, cannot or n't (its apostrophe straight, curly or U+02BC, or left out of a common contraction such as `isnt`) among the four words before it, within 200 characters, on its line and in its clause, or with `without`, `instead of` or `rather than` directly before it. `AI-only coverage decisions` (a hyphen), `the model alone decides whether a benefit applies` (a clause in between) and a decision with a negation of something else among those four words (`If not reviewed, the AI alone decides coverage`) are not matched.
rules.remediation: Require human sign-off on coverage decisions; disclose AI involvement to the consumer.
rules.title: AI-only insurance coverage decision

rules.description: Text mentions patient / clinical / mental-health / therapy / diagnosis but the tool never explicitly says the responder is an AI. Multiple 2026 state laws (TN, WA, UT) expect clear AI disclosure in clinical interactions.
rules.limitations: Reads `.md`, `.json`, `.yaml`, `.yml` and `.txt` files. Healthcare context is one of nine words (`patient`, `clinical`, `medical`, `mental health`, `therapy`, `diagnosis`, `symptom`, `treatment`, `medication`) or its plural, except `diagnoses`, which is also a verb, and `symptoms`: on the 892-repo instruction-file slice its only match was engineering prose. A persona about a nurse, a prescription or a dosage is skipped, as is one that names only `diagnoses` or `symptoms`.
rules.remediation: Add a visible 'You are talking to an AI; this is not medical advice and is not a substitute for licensed care' disclosure.
rules.title: Healthcare context without explicit AI-disclosure to user

rules.description: A healthcare AI surface mentions suicide / self-harm / crisis but never references 988 / 911 / 112 / 999 / a crisis line. Tennessee HB 1951 (2026) creates criminal liability for encouraging suicide; lacking an escalation path materially worsens the exposure.
rules.limitations: Reads `.md`, `.json`, `.yaml`, `.yml` and `.txt` files and matches `suicid*`, `self-harm`, `overdose`, `harm myself`, `kill yourself`, `end my life` and similar; `want to die`, `self-injury` and `hurting themselves` are not matched. The escalation check passes on any `988`, `911`, `crisis line`, `emergency services` or `call 112` anywhere in the file, an unrelated number such as `ORD-911` included.
rules.remediation: Add explicit crisis-line escalation instructions in the prompt / system message; test for the most common suicide / self-harm phrases and escalate before generating any other reply.
rules.title: Crisis keywords handled without escalation path

rules.description: A hook command contains network-capable tools (curl, wget, nc, etc.), or an `http` hook posts each event to a URL that is cleartext to another machine, a bare IP address or carries a credential. Hooks run automatically and can exfiltrate code, API keys, or session data.
rules.limitations: Matches curl, wget, nc, ncat, ssh, scp, rsync and ftp by name, and the one-liners `python -c ... import requests` (not `python3 -c`) and `node -e ... fetch(`, in the command line of each hook (its `command`, followed by `args` when set). An `http` hook, which posts the event to its `url`, is reported when the URL, read both the way Node reads it and the way urlsplit and curl do, is plain http to a host other than this machine, names a bare IP address other than loopback, or carries a credential that evidence redaction masks (a password or token in the userinfo, a credential-named query parameter such as `token`, or a known token format such as a Slack or Discord webhook path); one to an https URL on a DNS name in every reading is otherwise not reported, wherever it points. What a script file does is not followed, so `bash .claude/hooks/report.sh` passes even when the script runs curl. Hooks are read from `.claude/settings.json`, `.claude/settings.local.json`, a plugin's `hooks/hooks.json` (where the plugin's directory holds `.claude-plugin/` or sits under a marketplace's `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`) and the frontmatter of a `SKILL.md`. A plugin or skill file over 512,000 bytes is not read. One nested too deeply to parse (YAML past 100 levels, or past 64 levels of `[ ]` or `{ }`, or JSON past 500 levels), or a frontmatter block that YAML aliases expand past twice its length plus 1,000 and past 200,000 nodes, is not read either, and the refusal is reported against the file as AAK-INTERNAL-SCANNER-FAIL. Hooks a plugin declares in `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` and hooks in a subagent's frontmatter are not read.
rules.remediation: Remove network calls from hooks. Use file-based logging if audit trail is needed. An `http` hook that must report somewhere should post to an https URL on a host name you control, with any credential in a header taken from `allowedEnvVars` rather than in the URL.
rules.title: Hook executes network-capable command

rules.description: A hook command accesses credential environment variables, or an `http` hook sends one in a header. This enables direct credential theft via hook execution.
rules.limitations: Matches four names written as a bare `$NAME` (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID) and three exfiltration pipelines in a hook's command line, and an `http` hook that sends one of the four: a `headers` value that interpolates it (`$NAME` or `${NAME}`) while `allowedEnvVars` lists it. `$HOME` and `$PATH` are not credentials and are not reported. In a command line the braced form `${ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}` is not matched, and in a command or a header neither is any other credential variable (`$GITHUB_TOKEN`): an `http` hook that sends a token of its own (`$HOOK_TOKEN`) is authenticating to the endpoint it reports to. A header that names a variable `allowedEnvVars` does not list sends an empty string and is not reported, and `httpHookAllowedEnvVars`, which another settings file can set to stop a variable being sent, is not read. Hooks a plugin declares in `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` and hooks in a subagent's frontmatter are not read.
rules.remediation: Take the variable out of the hook command. The rule matches `$ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `$OPENAI_API_KEY`, `$AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` and `$AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, and the pipelines `env | curl`, `printenv | nc` and `echo $VAR | base64`. Let the program the hook runs read its own credentials from its environment. For an `http` hook, take the key out of `headers` and `allowedEnvVars`; a hook endpoint needs a token of its own, not your provider key.
rules.title: Hook command contains environment variable exfiltration

rules.description: A hook command writes to paths outside the project boundary, which can modify system configs, plant persistence, or stage exfiltration.
rules.limitations: Reads the hook's command line as shell commands and reports one that writes a path under /tmp, ~, /etc, /var, /usr or /home: a `>` or `>>` redirect, `tee`, `mkdir`, `touch`, `chmod`, `chown` or `truncate` on it, the destination of `cp`, `mv`, `install` or `ln`, `sed -i` or `perl -i`, `curl -o`, `wget -O` or `-P`, `dd of=`, or `tar` creating or extracting there, also inside `sh -c` and after `sudo` or `env`. A command that only names such a path (`cd /tmp/build`, reading `~/.config`) is not reported, and neither is deleting one. A path reached through `$HOME` or a relative climb (`../../shared/out.json`) is not matched, nor is a write made by a script the hook runs. Hooks a plugin declares in `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` and hooks in a subagent's frontmatter are not read.
rules.remediation: Write only inside the project: use project-relative paths for anything the hook creates or changes. The rule reports a write to a path under `/tmp`, `~`, `/etc`, `/var`, `/usr` or `/home`, such as a `>` redirect, `tee`, `cp`, `mv`, `sed -i`, `curl -o` or `tar`; calling a tool by its absolute path, or reading such a path, does not fire it.
rules.title: Hook command writes to files outside project directory

rules.description: A hook runs a command on PreToolUse, PostToolUse, SessionStart or UserPromptSubmit, so it runs automatically around tool calls, on every prompt and at session start. This is an inventory entry, not evidence of harm: the rule reads only the event and whether the command names a formatter, not what the command or a script it calls does. Review what it runs.
rules.limitations: Fires only for a hook on PreToolUse, PostToolUse, SessionStart or UserPromptSubmit whose command names none of a list of formatters. The same command on any other event, such as Stop, is not reported, and a command that merely contains a formatter name anywhere, even in a trailing comment (`# prettier`), counts as a formatter. A hook that runs no command (`http`, `prompt`, `agent`, `mcp_tool`) is not reported on any event. Hooks a plugin declares in `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` and hooks in a subagent's frontmatter are not read.
rules.remediation: Review what the command runs, including any script it calls. Keep the hooks you can account for and remove the rest.
rules.title: Hook runs a command on tool use, prompt submit or session start

rules.description: A hook command contains base64 operations, commonly used to obfuscate exfiltration payloads or encode stolen credentials.
rules.limitations: Matches the words base64, btoa, atob, b64encode and b64decode in a hook command. Other encodings that hide a payload the same way, hex through `xxd -r -p` or `base32 -d`, are not matched. Hooks a plugin declares in `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` and hooks in a subagent's frontmatter are not read.
rules.remediation: Remove base64 operations from hooks unless there's a documented, legitimate use case.
rules.title: Hook command uses base64 encoding/decoding

rules.description: A hook command uses sudo, doas, pkexec, or chmod +x. Hooks should never require elevated privileges.
rules.limitations: Matches sudo, doas, pkexec and `chmod` followed by whitespace and `+x`. `chmod 755`, `chmod a+x` and `su root -c`, which grant the same execute or root rights, are not matched. Hooks a plugin declares in `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` and hooks in a subagent's frontmatter are not read.
rules.remediation: Remove `sudo`, `doas`, `pkexec` and `chmod +x` from the hook command. A hook needs no elevated rights; to run a script, commit it with its executable bit set (`git update-index --chmod=+x script.sh`) instead of changing the mode from the hook.
rules.title: Hook command runs with elevated privileges

rules.description: More than 15 hook definitions in a single settings file. Large hook surface increases audit burden and risk of hidden malicious hooks.
rules.limitations: Counts the hooks of all events in one file (a settings file, a plugin's `hooks/hooks.json` or a `SKILL.md`), each hook in a `matcher` group's `hooks` array separately, and fires above 15. Hooks split between files, such as `.claude/settings.json` and `.claude/settings.local.json`, are not added up, and hooks a plugin declares in `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` or a subagent in its frontmatter are not counted.
rules.remediation: Remove hooks that are not essential, or fold related ones into one script, until each file has 15 or fewer hooks. The rule counts every hook, each one in a matcher group's `hooks` array on its own, in each settings file, plugin `hooks/hooks.json` and `SKILL.md` separately, and fires above 15.
rules.title: Excessive number of hooks defined

rules.description: A hook command contains hex-encoded strings, unicode escapes, an embedded base64 blob or nested shell invocations. Obfuscation is a strong indicator of malicious intent.
rules.limitations: Matches `\x41` and `\u0041` escapes, `sh -c` twice in one command (inside `bash -c` too), and an unbroken run of 64 or more letters, digits, `+` or `=` that mixes upper case, lower case and digits, as base64 does. A hex digest (an image pinned `@sha256:`) and a long readable command are not reported, and a base64 blob whose `/` characters split it into runs shorter than 64 is missed. The same text written as bash octal escapes (`$'\143\165\162\154'`) or reassembled from shell variables (`$a$b`) is not matched. Hooks a plugin declares in `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` and hooks in a subagent's frontmatter are not read.
rules.remediation: Rewrite the hook so its command is plain: remove `\xNN` and `\uNNNN` escapes and nested `sh -c ... sh -c` chains, and replace an embedded base64 blob (64 or more letters, digits, `+` or `=` in a row, mixing upper case, lower case and digits) with the command it encodes, or with a script file in the repository that the hook calls by path, where it can be reviewed. Length alone does not fire the rule.
rules.title: Hook command contains obfuscated or encoded payload

rules.description: A hook command reads or references project source code files, which could enable code exfiltration.
rules.limitations: Matches a file a reader command reads: an operand of cat, head, tail, less or more, a file operand of grep, sed or awk (never the pattern or program), or a `< file` redirect, ending in a lower-case .py, .js, .ts, .go, .rs, .java, .rb, .c, .cpp or .h, also inside `sh -c`. A pattern that names an extension (`grep '\.py$'`) is not a read. Archiving or copying source (`tar czf out.tgz src/`, `cp src/main.py out/`) and reading a file of another type (`cat src/App.tsx`) are not matched. Hooks a plugin declares in `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` and hooks in a subagent's frontmatter are not read.
rules.remediation: Remove the `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `less`, `more`, `grep`, `sed` or `awk` call, or the `<` redirect, that reads a `.py`, `.js`, `.ts`, `.go`, `.rs`, `.java`, `.rb`, `.c`, `.cpp` or `.h` file in the hook command. If the hook needs the source for a check, run the project's own linter or formatter on the file instead of reading its contents.
rules.title: Hook command references project source files

rules.description: A Claude Code hook script command-string interpolates a variable or captured group directly into a shell command. This is the CVE-2025-59536 shape: a poisoned config file triggers arbitrary code execution.
rules.limitations: Reads command strings in the Claude Code settings files, and .sh, .bash, .py, .js, .ts or .mjs scripts under a `hooks` directory inside `.claude/`, looking for `${`, `$(`, a backtick, `{{`, `%{` or a string `+` directly before a name beginning input, args, event, payload, user, argv or request. In a .py, .js, .ts or .mjs script that counts only when the same file also contains one of the texts `subprocess.<name>`, `os.system`, `os.popen`, `commands.getoutput`, `child_process`, `execSync`, `spawnSync`, the word `exec` or `execa`, `spawn(`, `Deno.run`, `sh -c`, `bash -c` or `os.exec`, called or not, so a wrapper such as `execute(...)` does not count. The same script kept outside `.claude/hooks/` (`scripts/guard.sh`) or under another extension (`guard.zsh`) is not read, and a plain `$cmd` filled from `jq` is not matched. A settings file over 1 MB, or a hook script over 512 KB, is not read.
rules.remediation: Never interpolate hook input into a shell string. Use an argv list and a no-shell exec. Quote with shlex.quote if a shell is absolutely required.
rules.title: Hook command interpolates user-controlled input

rules.description: A hook script invokes subprocess.run / spawn with shell=True (or the equivalent in Node/Bash) while passing a composed string that includes caller-provided fields.
rules.limitations: Matches `shell=True` before the first closing parenthesis of a `subprocess.run`, `call`, `Popen` or `check_output` call, and `shell: true` as any option of a Node `spawn`, `spawnSync`, `child_process.exec` or `child_process.execSync` call (`{ cwd: dir, shell: true }`), in a .sh, .bash, .py, .js, .ts or .mjs script under `.claude/.../hooks/`. A call with another call ahead of the option (`subprocess.run(build(cmd), shell=True)`, `spawn(String(cmd), [], { shell: true })`), a quoted key (`{ "shell": true }`), `shell: true` passed to `execFile` or to `exec` called by its bare name, `subprocess.check_call`, and `os.system` and `os.popen`, which always use a shell, are not matched. A settings file over 1 MB, or a hook script over 512 KB, is not read.
rules.remediation: Use shell=False and pass argv as a list. If a shell is needed, build commands from quoted constants only.
rules.title: Hook runs with shell=True and variable interpolation

rules.description: Claude Code (`@anthropic-ai/claude-code`, npm) shows a startup trust dialog before it acts on what a project carries, such as the hooks in its `.claude/settings.json`. Before 1.0.111, a bug in that dialog meant Claude Code "could be tricked to execute code contained in a project before the user accepted the startup trust dialog", so starting it in a cloned repository was enough (CVE-2025-59536, CVSS 4.0 8.7, CWE-94, GHSA-4fgq-fpq9-mr3g). This pin-only rule fires on a declared `@anthropic-ai/claude-code` below 1.0.111. Until 2026-10-17 it fired on any command in a `settings.local.json` instead, which cannot show whether a hook runs before the dialog: the release decides that. Auto-update has delivered the fix to installs that keep it on.
rules.limitations: Reports `@anthropic-ai/claude-code` below 1.0.111 where a project states its version: a package.json or lockfile entry at the root, or a versioned `npx` reference in an MCP config. An unpinned reference is not reported, as for the other Claude Code pins: it resolves to the newest release, and the CLI updates itself. A global install, the usual one, is in no file AAK reads, and neither is a package.json in a sub-directory. A file over 2 MB, or a lockfile over 32 MiB, is not read. Settings files and hook commands are not read: whether a hook runs before the trust dialog depends on the release, not on the hook. A declaration nested more than 64 levels deep in package.json, a TOML manifest or an MCP config (an MCP server more than 62) is still judged, and reported without a line; a lockfile entry keeps its line at any depth.
rules.remediation: Upgrade `@anthropic-ai/claude-code` to 1.0.111 or later and pin it, or leave auto-update on.
rules.title: Claude Code below 1.0.111 runs project code before the trust dialog (CVE-2025-59536)

rules.description: A task in `.vscode/tasks.json` sets `runOptions.runOn: folderOpen`, so it runs as soon as the folder is opened — before any human interaction and before the workspace-trust prompt. This is the vector the keyv npm worm used to spread: a poisoned repository executes code the instant a victim opens it. Severity is high on its own and critical when the auto-run command is a shell, an interpreter, or a network fetch.
rules.limitations: Reads the `tasks` array of `.vscode/tasks.json` for `runOptions.runOn: folderOpen`. A task declared in the `tasks` block of a workspace file (`*.code-workspace`) is not read. A `tasks.json` or `launch.json` over 1 MB is not read.
rules.remediation: Remove `runOn: folderOpen` from any task that runs a command, or gate the task behind an explicit manual trigger. Never auto-run a shell, interpreter, or network-fetch command on folder open; require workspace trust first.
rules.title: VS Code task auto-executes on folderOpen (pre-trust code execution)

rules.description: A task in `.vscode/tasks.json` builds its `command`/`args` in a way that reaches a shell: a pipe-to-shell (`... | sh`), an interpreter invoked on a script path inside the repo, or a `${...}`/interpolated variable spliced into a shell string. A poisoned repository controls that string, so opening or running the task executes attacker-chosen code.
rules.limitations: Judges a task by its own `command` and `args` text: a pipe into sh, bash, zsh, dash, ksh, fish, pwsh or powershell; python, python2, python3, node, deno, bun, ruby, perl, php, bash, sh or zsh followed directly by a path of letters, digits, `_`, `-`, `.`, `/` and `\` that ends .py, .js, .cjs, .mjs, .ts, .rb, .pl, .php, .sh, .bash, .zsh or .ps1, where the path may start with the workspace folder as `${workspaceFolder}`, `${workspaceFolder:name}`, `${workspaceRoot}` or `${fileWorkspaceFolder}`; or `${`, `%{`, `{{`, `$(`, a backtick or a string `+` directly before a name beginning input, args, event, payload, user, argv or request. A script run directly (`./scripts/setup.sh`), through a runner (`npm run setup`) or after a flag (`bash -x ./scripts/setup.sh`), and a quoted path (`bash "${workspaceFolder}/scripts/setup.sh"`), are not followed. A `tasks.json` or `launch.json` over 1 MB is not read.
rules.remediation: Do not pipe downloaded content into a shell and do not interpolate variables into shell command strings. Invoke a vetted, in-tree binary with a fixed argv, and pin or verify any script the task runs.
rules.title: VS Code task command reaches a shell via pipe, repo-path interpreter, or interpolation

rules.description: A configuration in `.vscode/launch.json` sets `preLaunchTask` to a task that AAK flagged (a folderOpen auto-run or a shell-reaching command). Starting a debug session then runs that task, so the launch config is a second trigger for the same code-execution path. Reported as one finding naming both files.
rules.limitations: Matches a launch configuration's `preLaunchTask` by label against tasks that AAK-IDE-TASK-001 or AAK-IDE-TASK-002 flagged in the `tasks.json` next to it. A `preLaunchTask` that names a compound task (`dependsOn: ["setup"]`) reaches the same script but is not matched, and `postDebugTask` is not read. A `tasks.json` or `launch.json` over 1 MB is not read.
rules.remediation: Point `preLaunchTask` only at tasks that run vetted, fixed-argv commands. Remove the auto-run or shell injection from the referenced task (see the paired AAK-IDE-TASK-001 / AAK-IDE-TASK-002 finding).
rules.title: VS Code launch.json preLaunchTask chains to a flagged auto-exec task

rules.description: A `.vscode/tasks.json` or `.vscode/launch.json` file could not be parsed even after stripping JSONC comments and trailing commas. AAK reports this rather than skipping it silently: an unparseable config file is exactly where an auto-run task would hide from a scan.
rules.limitations: Parses only `tasks.json` and `launch.json` directly inside a `.vscode` folder. A broken `.vscode/settings.json`, or a `.code-workspace` file, which can carry a `tasks` block of its own, is not parsed and never reported. A `tasks.json` or `launch.json` over 1 MB is not read.
rules.remediation: Fix the JSON/JSONC syntax so the file can be audited. If it is intentionally not a VS Code task/launch config, move it out of `.vscode/`.
rules.title: VS Code task/launch config could not be parsed

rules.description: A 12-digit Aadhaar number passed the Verhoeff checksum and is embedded in project text. Aadhaar is restricted under the UIDAI Act and India DPDP §8(4). Storing in code is a reportable breach.
rules.limitations: Reads source, config and text files by extension (`.py`, `.ts`, `.json`, `.yaml`, `.toml`, `.ini`, `.txt`, `.md` and a few more) and env files (`.env`, `.env.local`) for a Verhoeff-valid Aadhaar number. Any other extension is never opened: the rows of a customer export saved as `.csv` are not reported, while the same rows in a `.txt` file are.
rules.remediation: Remove the Aadhaar number. If Aadhaar is genuinely needed, route it through an encrypted vault (e.g. AWS KMS / Azure Key Vault) and never log or commit it.
rules.title: Aadhaar number in source / config

rules.description: A 10-char PAN (5 letters + 4 digits + 1 letter) was detected. PAN is tax-linked personal data under DPDP §8(4).
rules.limitations: Reads a PAN written in capitals: five letters, four digits and a letter. The same PAN in lower case (`abcde1234f`) is not reported.
rules.remediation: Remove the PAN. If needed for processing, tokenize it and store tokens, not raw PANs.
rules.title: PAN (Permanent Account Number) in source / config

rules.description: A UPI VPA (<handle>@<psp>) was detected. UPI IDs are payment identifiers regulated by NPCI and covered by DPDP §8(4).
rules.limitations: Reads a UPI ID only when the handle after the `@` is one of fifteen payment-app handles (`@oksbi`, `@ybl`, `@paytm`, `@upi` and eleven more). An ID at any other handle, such as `@kotak`, is not reported.
rules.remediation: Remove the UPI ID. Accept UPI addresses as runtime input only.
rules.title: UPI ID in source / config

rules.description: An IFSC code (4 letters + 0 + 6 alnum) was detected. IFSC is a banking identifier; pairing it with an account number constitutes DPDP §8(4) 'sensitive personal data'.
rules.limitations: Reads an IFSC code written in capitals: four letters, a `0` and six letters or digits. The same code in lower case (`sbin0001234`) is not reported.
rules.remediation: Move IFSC codes out of source; look them up at runtime from RBI's public IFSC directory.
rules.title: IFSC code in source / config

rules.description: An Indian +91 mobile number (starting 6/7/8/9) was detected. Phone numbers are personal data under DPDP §8(4).
rules.limitations: Reads a `+91` mobile number whose ten digits follow the country code without a break (`+91 9876543210`). The same number grouped in fives, `+91 98765 43210`, is not reported.
rules.remediation: Remove the phone number. Never log raw phone numbers — hash them.
rules.title: Indian mobile number in source / config

rules.description: An Indian state-issued vehicle registration (e.g. 'MH 12 AB 1234') was detected. Vehicle registrations are PII in combination with driver records.
rules.limitations: Reads a registration only when it starts with one of 37 state and territory codes (`MH`, `DL`, `KA`, `TS` and so on). A code that is not on the list is not reported, and the list has no `TG`, the code Telangana has issued since 2024 in place of `TS`.
rules.remediation: Remove the registration from source. If dealing with vehicle data, anonymize before checking in.
rules.title: Indian vehicle registration in source / config

rules.description: A scanner did not finish its work on every file, so the rules it owns were not evaluated where it stopped, and the results are incomplete. Either the scanner crashed, which is a bug in agent-audit-kit itself and costs its findings on every file (please file an issue with the evidence string), or it refused one file it could not read or parse safely, which costs that file alone. Either way the scan went on with every other scanner. The pin-drift scanner reports here, against the file, when `.agent-audit-kit/tool-pins.json` exists but cannot be read: a rug-pull check with no readable baseline has checked nothing, and the evidence says why the file could not be used. Any scanner reports here, against one file, when it refuses that file: a JSON or JSONC file nested past 500 levels (Python's own parser stops at a depth that differs by version, and every version refuses past this; real configs nest under 20), one nested deeper than Python's TOML or Python parser takes (before Python 3.11, whose parser has no depth check, a Python source a linear screen bounds past 10,000 levels is refused before it is parsed; one under that bound is parsed, and costs what a source of its size does: up to about 40 s of CPU for 500 KB on 3.9, deep or not), a TOML key of more than 64 dotted parts (tomllib builds a dotted key one part at a time, at a cost that grows with the square of the parts, so the file is refused before it is parsed), a TOML file holding an integer Python cannot convert (one past 4,300 digits, the limit `int()` has had since 3.9.14, 3.10.7 and 3.11; a JSON file reads such an integer as the nearest float and a YAML file as its text, so neither is refused), a Python syntax tree deeper than the scanner's walk takes (a walk runs with a recursion limit of 10,000 frames, about 3,300 levels for the walk that takes the most frames a level; the deepest of 100,303 real files has 569), or YAML nested past 100 levels, or past 64 levels of `[ ]` or `{ }`, or grown by its aliases past their bound. The scanner went on with every other file, and the evidence names the scanner, the file and the reason.
rules.remediation: If the evidence names an input file, repair it. For the tool-pin file, restore it from version control, or review the current tool definitions and re-pin with `agent-audit-kit pin`; re-pinning accepts whatever the config declares now, so review first. Otherwise file an issue at https://github.com/sattyamjjain/agent-audit-kit/issues with the scanner name, exception class, and (if safe) the project shape.
rules.title: A scanner did not finish every file

rules.description: A source / config file (`.md`, `.txt`, `.yml`, `.yaml`, `.json`, `.py`) embeds a known wild IPI payload from the 2026-04-24 Help Net Security + Infosec Magazine catalogue. Common shapes: ignore-prior + exfil, system-role override, reveal-system-prompt, credential exfil via cURL, tool-call rerouting, delete-repository, admin role escalation, obfuscated prompt break, image-attached IPI, RAG-poisoned document. Refresh the corpus with `aak corpus update --ipi`.
rules.limitations: Reads `.md`, `.txt`, `.yml`, `.yaml`, `.json` and `.py` files, by their lower-case extension, and applies ten regular expressions to the text, where `.*` does not cross a line. The same payload in `.jsonl`, `.html` or `.j2` (RAG seed corpora and prompt templates), in a `.MD` file, or split over two lines, is not matched. A file over 1 MB is not read.
rules.remediation: Remove the payload from the file. If the file is intentionally an attack-corpus fixture, exclude it via `--ignore-paths`. The real risk is checked-in poisoned templates / system-prompt files / RAG seed corpora — those need to be sanitized at ingestion time, not at scan time.
rules.title: Indirect-prompt-injection wild payload checked into repo

rules.description: A lockfile resolves, a manifest pins, or a site-packages directory has installed a PyPI or npm release that an OSV advisory lists as affected. vLLM 0.31.1 and MLflow 3.16.0 locked in a project passed every rule on 0.6.28 (28 Oct 2026), although CVEs against both were published on 26 and 27 Oct, because AAK knew a vulnerable release only through a hand-written pin. The rule reads the offline advisory feed `aak update` builds from the OSV exports it already downloads for the malicious-release feed: every PyPI and npm record that is not `MAL-` or withdrawn and has a range or a version list. A scan reads the copy cached at `~/.agent-audit-kit/advisories.json`, else the records bundled with AAK, and never touches the network. The finding carries the advisory's severity: CRITICAL from a CVSS 3.x base score of 9.0, HIGH from 7.0, MEDIUM below that or unscored, and INFO for a manifest range that admits affected and unaffected releases.
rules.limitations: Reads what AAK-MALICIOUS-RELEASE-001 reads, anywhere outside AAK's skip directories: the lockfiles uv.lock, poetry.lock, Pipfile.lock, package-lock.json, npm-shrinkwrap.json, pnpm-lock.yaml and yarn.lock (v1); declarations in requirements*.txt, pyproject.toml, Pipfile, package.json (not its `scripts`) and the launches in MCP configs; and `<name>-<version>.dist-info` directories in the site-packages and dist-packages directories AAK-STARTUP-HOOK-PTH-001's walk reaches. A release matches by PEP 440 order on PyPI (3.12.0rc0 is inside `>=3.12.0rc0`, 3.17.0rc1 below a 3.17.0 fix) and semver on npm, against the record's `ECOSYSTEM` and `SEMVER` ranges, read in version order, and its listed versions; a git range, a CVSS 4.0 vector and a record with no PyPI or npm package are not read, and a record scored by neither a CVSS 3.x vector nor GitHub's label is reported MEDIUM. A declaration without a version is not judged, and a range is read on release triples, as the pin table reads ranges, so a pre-release bound counts as its release. A range that admits affected and unaffected releases is one INFO finding naming at most five advisories, and none when a lockfile in the same directory resolves the package. A PYSEC record and its GHSA twin are one advisory, reported under the GHSA id; two GHSA records are never merged. Where another rule reports every CVE id of the advisory on the same line of the same file at or above this finding's severity, as most version pins do, only that rule's finding is kept; an advisory without a CVE id is always reported. A lockfile is read for its first 64 distinct releases of a package. The bundled records are the two OSV advisories of 27 and 28 Oct 2026 against vLLM and MLflow, so without `aak update` nothing else is known; a feed over 60 MB keeps only HIGH and CRITICAL records and says so. `.egg-info` installs, `node_modules`, conda metadata and image layers are not read. A manifest over 2 MB or a lockfile over 32 MiB is not read.
rules.remediation: Upgrade to the release the finding names as fixed on that line, re-lock, and rebuild the environment or image; for a manifest range, raise its lower bound past the fix. Where the advisory lists no fixed release, remove or replace the package, or keep the component the advisory names unreachable until one ships. Run `aak update` so the scan reads the current advisories rather than the bundled few.
rules.title: A locked, pinned or installed release is affected by a published advisory

rules.description: A Python manifest pins `langchain-core`, the PyPI distribution CVE-2026-34070 names (GHSA-qh6h-p6c9-ff54), below 1.2.22, or declares a range that admits a release below it. Before that release, load_prompt() and load_prompt_from_config() accept absolute paths and '..' traversal.
rules.limitations: Reads `langchain-core`, in any PEP 503 spelling, from requirements.txt, requirements-dev.txt, requirements-prod.txt and dev-requirements.txt at the project root and from every pyproject.toml, taking the lowest version a range allows. A git reference or an archive is judged by the release its tag or file name names (`@langchain-core==1.2.21`, `langchain_core-1.2.21.tar.gz`), with releases compared on their first three numbers, so a pre-release of the fix (`langchain-core==1.2.22rc1`) reads as the fix. A `langchain-core` that states no version, a git reference to a commit or a branch included (any name holding a `/` but `refs/tags/<tag>`, such as `release/1.2.21`), is not reported, and a lockfile (uv.lock, poetry.lock) or another requirements file (`requirements-test.txt`, `requirements/base.txt`) is not read. npm packages are not read: the advisory names only the PyPI distribution, and npm's `@langchain/*` packages have version lines of their own. The umbrella `langchain` and `langchain-community` distributions are not read either, because their version numbers are not langchain-core's, so a project that pins only those is not reported. Declarations of one install that no release satisfies together (`langchain-core==1.2.22` beside `langchain-core==1.2.21` in one requirements file) admit nothing and are not reported; pip refuses to install them too. A pyproject.toml that does not parse and a manifest over 2 MB are not read. A pyproject.toml with a key of more than 64 dotted parts, or holding an integer Python cannot convert (one past 4,300 digits), is refused and reported as AAK-INTERNAL-SCANNER-FAIL.
rules.remediation: Upgrade to langchain-core >= 1.2.22. If you must keep the legacy behavior, pass allow_dangerous_paths=True explicitly.
rules.title: Project depends on langchain-core < 1.2.22 (load_prompt path traversal)

rules.description: Source code calls langchain.load_prompt() or load_prompt_from_config() with a user-controlled path argument. Even on patched versions, the allow_dangerous_paths escape hatch is a sharp edge.
rules.limitations: Pattern-matches the first `load_prompt(` or `load_prompt_from_config(` call in a file that mentions langchain, and only when the argument is a bare (dotted) name or an f-string with a `{}` placeholder. An argument that is a call (`os.path.join(PROMPTS, name)`), a concatenation (`"prompts/" + name`) or a keyword (`path=name`) is not matched. A requirements file or pyproject.toml over 2 MB is not read. A pyproject.toml with a key of more than 64 dotted parts, or holding an integer Python cannot convert (one past 4,300 digits), is refused and reported as AAK-INTERNAL-SCANNER-FAIL.
rules.remediation: Treat load_prompt() as a file read against a trusted root. Resolve, normalize, and verify the path is inside the intended directory.
rules.title: Call to load_prompt without allow_dangerous_paths review

rules.description: A Python manifest pins `langchain-core` below 0.3.14. CVE-2025-68664 (GHSA-c67j-w6g6-q2cm) is a serialization-injection chain in langchain-core's dumps/loads that extracts secrets through crafted saved chains.
rules.limitations: Reads `langchain-core` from the same Python manifests as AAK-LANGCHAIN-001, never npm. The floor is the rule's original 0.3.14, below the advisory's fixes, which are 0.3.81 on 0.3 and 1.2.5 on 1.x, so langchain-core 0.3.14 to 0.3.80 and 1.0.0 to 1.2.4 are affected and not reported. Every version below 0.3.14 is also below AAK-LANGCHAIN-001's 1.2.22, which does report it. LangChain.js has a separate advisory, which no rule cites. A requirements file or pyproject.toml over 2 MB is not read. A pyproject.toml with a key of more than 64 dotted parts, or holding an integer Python cannot convert (one past 4,300 digits), is refused and reported as AAK-INTERNAL-SCANNER-FAIL.
rules.remediation: Upgrade langchain-core to 0.3.81 or later on the 0.3 line, or to 1.2.5 or later on 1.x, and pin it. Avoid loading serialized chains from sources you do not fully control.
rules.title: LangChain deserialization of untrusted data

rules.description: `langchain.prompts.load_prompt(path)` / `PromptTemplate.from_file(path)` accepts an attacker-influenced path without anchoring to a project root or allow-listed URI scheme. CVE-2026-34070 (CVSS 7.5): the lc:// scheme + raw file paths let a crafted prompt template read arbitrary files. Patched in `langchain-core>=0.3.74`; pinning a vulnerable version is also a finding.
rules.limitations: Needs a non-constant path passed to `load_prompt` or `from_file` and, in the same function, a source spelled `request.json`, `request.args`, `sys.argv`, `os.environ` or the like; a path that arrives as a function parameter is not a source. Any `os.path.realpath(` in the function counts as a guard although it normalises the path and does not confine it to a directory. A file that imports `from langchain_core.prompts.loading import load_prompt` is skipped. A Python file over 512 KB is not read.
rules.remediation: Validate every prompt path with `agent_audit_kit.checks.path_under_root(path, root)` before calling load_prompt. For S3 / HTTP backed prompt stores, prefer the explicit `langchain_community.storage.*` adapters; AAK exempts those via pattern-not-inside. Bump `langchain-core` to >= 0.3.74.
rules.title: LangChain load_prompt path traversal (CVE-2026-34070)

rules.description: A function calls a known SSRF guard helper (`validate_safe_url`, `is_safe_url`, `validateSafeUrl`, etc.) and then fetches the same URL via `requests.get`, `httpx.get`, `urllib.request.urlopen`, `fetch`, or similar without disabling redirects. The allow-list fires once on the initial URL, but `requests` follows 3xx by default — a redirect into `http://169.254.169.254/...`, `http://localhost`, or another blocked target bypasses the guard and pulls the response back into the calling context. CVE-2026-41481 is the in-tree example (langchain-text-splitters < 1.1.2). Same shape applies in any agent-tooling code that does validate→fetch without `allow_redirects=False` / `follow_redirects=False` / `redirect: 'manual'`.
rules.limitations: In Python it looks inside one function for a call to one of seven guard names (`validate_safe_url`, `validate_url`, `is_safe_url`, `ensure_safe_url`, `check_safe_url`, `ssrf_guard`, `is_url_safe`) followed by a fetch (`get`, `post`, `put`, `delete`, `request`, `urlopen`, `fetch` or `send`) that does not disable redirects. A guard under another name (`assert_public_url`), or a guard and a fetch in two separate, non-nested Python functions, is not matched. The version check judges a git reference or an archive by the release its tag or file name names, with releases compared on their first three numbers, so a pre-release of the fix (`langchain-text-splitters==1.1.2rc1`) reads as the fix; a git reference to a commit or a branch (any name holding a `/` but `refs/tags/<tag>`) states no version and is reported. Declarations of one install that no release satisfies together (`langchain-text-splitters==1.1.2` beside `langchain-text-splitters==1.1.1` in one requirements file) admit nothing and are not reported; pip refuses to install them too. A source file over 1 MB, a pyproject.toml that does not parse and a manifest over 2 MB are not read. A pyproject.toml with a key of more than 64 dotted parts, or holding an integer Python cannot convert (one past 4,300 digits), is refused and reported as AAK-INTERNAL-SCANNER-FAIL. A lockfile over 32 MiB is not read.
rules.remediation: Disable redirect following on the fetch call: `requests.get(url, allow_redirects=False)`, `httpx.get(url, follow_redirects=False)`, `fetch(url, { redirect: 'manual' })`. Or revalidate the URL on every redirect hop. For `langchain-text-splitters`, bump to >= 1.1.2.
rules.title: Validate-then-fetch SSRF (redirects enabled past allow-list)

rules.description: Source code calls `ToolNode([...])` (or `ToolNode(some_list)`) with a positional list rather than the documented `ToolNode(tools=[...])` keyword form. langgraph-prebuilt 1.0.11 (2026-04-24) regressed and silently coerces a positional list into a single-tool node, dropping every tool past the first and producing message-loop bugs in agents that depend on tool-routing behaviour.
rules.limitations: Fires on `ToolNode(...)` with a list literal or a bare name as its first positional argument, in a file that imports langgraph.prebuilt as `from langgraph.prebuilt import ... ToolNode` on one line, `from langgraph import prebuilt` or `import langgraph.prebuilt`. A parenthesised multi-line import, `from langgraph.prebuilt.tool_node import ToolNode`, and an argument that is an attribute or a call (`ToolNode(self.tools)`) are not matched. A Python file over 512 KB is not read.
rules.remediation: Switch every `ToolNode([t1, t2, ...])` to `ToolNode(tools=[t1, t2, ...])`. `aak fix` rewrites the list-literal form in place, through the codemod at `agent_audit_kit/autofix/langgraph_toolnode.py` (`aak fix --dry-run` lists the change first); a bare name, `ToolNode(tools_list)`, is left for you to change.
rules.title: langgraph.prebuilt.ToolNode positional-list misuse

rules.description: A package.json in the project declares a copyleft license (AGPL, SSPL, GPL-3 or EUPL) in its `license` field. The rule reads the project's own manifests, not the dependencies it installs. Distributing that package, or offering it as a network service under AGPL or SSPL, carries the license's obligations.
rules.limitations: Reads the `license` field of each `package.json` in the scanned tree and matches a value that starts with `AGPL`, `SSPL`, `GPL-3` or `EUPL`. `node_modules` is skipped, so the license of an installed dependency is not checked, and the legacy `licenses` array is not read.
rules.remediation: Confirm that the declared license is the one the package should ship under, and that its obligations suit how the project is distributed or hosted. Installed dependencies are not checked here: run a license checker over the resolved dependency tree for those.
rules.title: Copyleft license (AGPL, SSPL, GPL-3 or EUPL) declared in package.json

rules.description: A package.json in the project has no `license` field, so the package states no terms under which others may use it. The rule reads the project's own manifests, not the dependencies it installs.
rules.limitations: Reads the `license` key of each `package.json` in the scanned tree and skips `node_modules`, so an installed dependency with no license is not checked. Any value counts as declared, an empty string and `UNLICENSED` included.
rules.remediation: Add a `license` field to the package.json: an SPDX identifier such as `MIT`, or `UNLICENSED` for a private package that grants no rights to others.
rules.title: package.json declares no license

rules.description: A dependency has been flagged for DMCA/IP violations or contains leaked proprietary code.
rules.limitations: Matches three package names (`claude-code-leaked`, `anthropic-internal` and `copilot-source`, with or without a scope) in the direct dependency maps of each `package.json`. An `npm:` alias (`"cc-tools": "npm:claude-code-leaked@^1.0.0"`), a lockfile entry, a Python requirement and any other name are not matched.
rules.remediation: Remove the flagged dependency immediately.
rules.title: DMCA-flagged package detected
