rules.description: Google MCP Toolbox for Databases (googleapis/mcp-toolbox), which MCP clients start through the npm launcher `@toolbox-sdk/server`, checks the local paths its Cloud Storage tools read and write (`download_object`, `upload_object`, and the `allowedLocalRoots` option from 1.5.0) lexically, with `filepath.Clean` and `filepath.Rel`, and never resolves symlinks. A caller allowed to run those tools can follow a link inside a permitted root to read or overwrite files outside it (CVE-2026-102242, CVSS 4.0 8.6, CWE-22/CWE-59). 1.10.0 resolves links with `filepath.EvalSymlinks` before the check (googleapis/mcp-toolbox#3810).
rules.limitations: Reports an npm reference to `@toolbox-sdk/server` from 1.2.0 up to 1.10.0: a package.json or lockfile entry, or the launcher in an MCP config, where an unpinned `npx @toolbox-sdk/server` is reported as unpinned, as for the other npm pins. The launcher runs the binary of its own version (`@toolbox-sdk/server-<os>-<arch>`), so its number is the server's. A toolbox binary started by path, or the container image, states no version AAK reads and is not reported. A file over 2 MB, or a lockfile over 32 MiB, is not read. A declaration nested more than 64 levels deep in package.json, a TOML manifest or an MCP config (an MCP server more than 62) is still judged, and reported without a line; a lockfile entry keeps its line at any depth.
rules.remediation: Upgrade `@toolbox-sdk/server`, and any toolbox binary or image, to 1.10.0 or later and pin it. Until then, on 1.5.0 to 1.9.x, set `allowedLocalRoots` and keep symlinks out of those directories; below 1.5.0 the option does not exist and the tools take any absolute path (CVE-2026-93328, reported as `AAK-MCP-TOOLBOX-CVE-2026-93328-001`), so only the upgrade helps.
rules.title: Google MCP Toolbox 1.2.0 to 1.9.0: local-path checks follow symlinks out of the allowed roots

rules.description: Google MCP Toolbox for Databases (googleapis/mcp-toolbox), which MCP clients start through the npm launcher `@toolbox-sdk/server`, has a Cloud Storage source from 1.2.0 whose tools take the bucket and the local path from the tool call. Before 1.5.0 nothing limits either: `upload_object` sends any file the server process can read to whatever bucket the call names, `download_object` writes over any file it can write, and `ValidateLocalPath` asks only for an absolute path with no `..` segment. Anyone who can invoke those tools can send host files to a bucket outside the project or overwrite local files (CVE-2026-93328, CVSS 4.0 9.3, CWE-22/CWE-862). 1.5.0 adds the `allowedBuckets` and `allowedLocalRoots` source options (googleapis/mcp-toolbox#3454), and both still allow everything when omitted.
rules.limitations: Reports an npm reference to `@toolbox-sdk/server` from 1.2.0 below 1.5.0 that states a version: a package.json or lockfile entry, or the launcher in an MCP config, reporting a range that admits an affected version. `latest` was 1.15.0 on 2026-10-27 and states no version, so an unversioned reference is not reported here (`AAK-MCP-TOOLBOX-CVE-2026-102242-001` reports one as unpinned). It reads the version, not the toolbox configuration: a server with no `cloud-storage` source is reported too, and 1.5.0 and later are not reported although a `cloud-storage` source that sets neither option is as exposed. The launcher runs the binary of its own version, so its number is the server's; a toolbox binary started by path, or the container image, states no version AAK reads and is not reported. 1.2.0 to 1.4.x also fire `AAK-MCP-TOOLBOX-CVE-2026-102242-001`. A file over 2 MB, or a lockfile over 32 MiB, is not read. A declaration nested more than 64 levels deep in package.json, a TOML manifest or an MCP config (an MCP server more than 62) is still judged, and reported without a line; a lockfile entry keeps its line at any depth.
rules.remediation: Upgrade `@toolbox-sdk/server`, and any toolbox binary or image, to 1.10.0 or later and pin it (1.5.0 adds the options; 1.10.0 also fixes CVE-2026-102242), then set `allowedBuckets` and `allowedLocalRoots` on every `cloud-storage` source: with either omitted, every bucket, or every absolute path the server process can reach, is allowed.
rules.title: Google MCP Toolbox 1.2.0 to 1.4.x: the Cloud Storage tools take any bucket and any local path

rules.description: An MCP server gates tools by an allowlist / read-only / non-destructive control (e.g. `ALLOWED_TOOLS`, `ALLOW_ONLY_NON_DESTRUCTIVE_TOOLS`, a `*READONLY*` / `*NON_DESTRUCTIVE*` env var or config) and applies that check in the tool-discovery handler (`tools/list` / `list_tools` / `ListToolsRequestSchema`) but NOT in the execution handler (`tools/call` / `call_tool` / `CallToolRequestSchema`). A client that skips discovery and calls a hidden tool name directly bypasses the control entirely — the gate is cosmetic. This is the CVE-2026-46519 class (mcp-server-kubernetes < 3.6.0 documented three env vars as access controls but enforced them only at the discovery layer; CWE-863 Incorrect Authorization, CVSS 8.8). This is an enforcement-layer asymmetry — distinct from AAK-MCPWN-001, which is a transport-middleware route asymmetry (`/mcp_message` vs `/mcp`). Do not conflate the two.
rules.limitations: In Python it compares the bodies of the functions named or decorated `list_tools` and `call_tool` (or dispatch, execute, run or invoke tool) for a fixed list of gate words (`allowed_tools`, `allow_only`, `read_only`, `readonly`, `non_destructive`, `destructive_tools`, `disable_destructive`). The gate has to be named in the list handler itself, so filtering done in a helper it calls, or under another name such as `TOOL_ALLOWLIST`, is not seen, and any mention of a gate word in the call handler, a log line included, counts as enforcing it.
rules.remediation: Enforce the same allowlist / read-only / non-destructive check inside the `tools/call` (execution) handler, not only in `tools/list` (discovery). Authorization must gate the action, not just its visibility — a denied tool must raise in the call path even when the client never listed it. Centralise the check (e.g. a shared `assert_tool_allowed(name)` called at the top of the call handler) so discovery and execution cannot drift apart.
rules.title: MCP tool gate enforced in tools/list but not tools/call

rules.description: An MCP client or aggregator assembles its tool catalogue from what upstream servers return, with no bound on the number of tools or the size of a schema. The size of the allocation is then chosen by whoever controls the upstream, not by this process. Distinct from an unbounded *request body*: that value arrives from the caller, this one arrives from the server being aggregated, and a body-size limit does not touch it.
rules.limitations: Detects the absence of any bound in the same file as the catalogue builder. A cap enforced in a wrapper or by the transport layer is not seen, and a slice, a length check, a max_* constant or a break in the loop all clear the finding.
rules.remediation: Cap the number of tools accepted from any single upstream and reject oversized descriptions and schemas before building the catalogue.
rules.title: MCP tool catalogue built from an upstream response with no cap

rules.description: ToolUniverse (`tooluniverse`, PyPI) through 1.2.6 runs caller-supplied Python inside a sandbox that can be escaped, on a server that requires no authentication (CVE-2026-81096, CVSS 10.0). The executor behind the `python_code_executor` tool inspects submitted source against a deny-list of attribute names and calls but leaves the attribute-lookup builtins available, so a dunder attribute reached through a string lookup — or through a module already permitted — lets a caller walk from a literal's class to its base and enumerate subclasses until it holds a reference to `subprocess`. A per-call argument also widens the import allow-list before the inspection runs. The HTTP and MCP servers (`http_api_server.py`, `smcp_server.py`) bind every interface with debugging enabled and no authentication, so any caller that reaches the port executes code as the server process. 1.3.0 adds bearer-token authentication, defaults the bind address to loopback, and hardens the attribute checks. Treat < 1.3.0 (and unpinned) as exposed.
rules.limitations: Dependency-level detection only: this fires on the pinned or unpinned `tooluniverse` reference, not on the sandbox-escape pattern itself. The pattern itself is covered by `AAK-SANDBOX-DENYLIST-001`, which shipped for issue #704 and fires on a deny-list of names checked against a value that is then executed in-process with a lookup primitive still reachable. A file over 2 MB, or a lockfile over 32 MiB, is not read. A declaration nested more than 64 levels deep in package.json, a TOML manifest or an MCP config (an MCP server more than 62) is still judged, and reported without a line; a lockfile entry keeps its line at any depth.
rules.remediation: Upgrade `tooluniverse` to >= 1.3.0 and pin it. Do not expose the code-executor tool on a non-loopback interface, and require authentication in front of it — a deny-list over attribute names is not a sandbox boundary.
rules.title: ToolUniverse unauthenticated RCE via python_code_executor sandbox escape (<= 1.2.6)

rules.description: An MCP server exposes an HTTP/SSE transport on every network interface and creates sessions without requiring a caller credential. A credential is present — read from the environment and attached to the server's own upstream requests — but it authenticates the server to its backend, not the caller to the server, so any host that can reach the listener invokes the full tool surface with the operator's stored token. The bind is often implicit: in Node, `.listen(port)` with the host argument omitted binds every interface with no 0.0.0.0 literal anywhere in the source.
rules.limitations: Reads one file at a time, so an inbound check applied from a separate middleware module is not seen. The implicit all-interfaces bind is inferred for JS/TS only, where Node's listen() defaults to every interface; Python servers default to loopback and are never inferred.
rules.remediation: Require a separate inbound credential for network transports, and treat environment tokens as outbound-only — never as proof of a caller's identity. Bind 127.0.0.1 by default, and set `enableDnsRebindingProtection: true` with `allowedHosts` / `allowedOrigins` on each transport (or use the SDK's `hostHeaderValidation()` middleware).
rules.title: MCP HTTP transport binds every interface and authenticates no caller

rules.description: Trinity (Abilityai/trinity) is a self-hosted agent platform whose backend ships as `ghcr.io/abilityai/trinity-backend`. An agent-scoped MCP API key resolves to the agent's owner, and the Telegram router's binding routes (`configure_telegram_bot` and `delete_telegram_binding` in `src/backend/routers/telegram.py`) check only that the caller owns the agent, with no `reject_agent_principal`. So an agent, typically steered by prompt injection, can perform what are meant to be human-only binding operations: in NVD's words, "send messages through the owner's bot token, replace the binding with their own token, or delete it" (CVE-2026-108756, CVSS 3.1 5.4, CWE-862). The images start at 0.9.5-rc1, 0.9.5 is the newest release, and the 1.0.0 release candidates still serve those routes without the check, so there is no fixed release.
rules.limitations: Reads `ghcr.io/abilityai/trinity-backend` references up to and including 0.9.5, and `latest`, which was the 0.9.5 digest on 2026-10-13, in compose files, Kubernetes manifests, Helm values, Dockerfiles and MCP configs. Trinity's own compose files build the backend from source or name it with `${TRINITY_IMAGE_TAG:-latest}`, which states no version this reader trusts, so such an instance is reported only where a manifest states the tag. The 1.0.0 release candidates read as 1.0.0 and are not reported, although they still lack the check, and the two-part `0.9` tag floats and is not reported.
rules.remediation: There is no fixed release. Until one ships, treat every agent on an instance with a Telegram binding as able to change that binding: remove the binding from agents that do not need it, and check the bound bot after any agent run that read untrusted content. Pin the first fixed release once it ships.
rules.title: Trinity backend image through 0.9.5: an agent's MCP key can replace or delete its owner's Telegram binding (no fixed release)

rules.description: The official MCP TypeScript SDK (`@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` on npm for 1.x, `@modelcontextprotocol/client` for 2.x) can act as an MCP client over HTTP with OAuth. From 1.12.0, when the client began reading the authorization server from the MCP server's protected resource metadata, until 1.31.0 and 2.2.0, stored and pre-provisioned credentials were not bound to the authorization server they belong to. A malicious or compromised MCP server could name its own authorization server, and with no user interaction the client sent it the `refresh_token` and `client_secret` stored from an earlier sign-in (1.x), or the `client_secret` or signed assertion of a bundled non-interactive provider (1.x and 2.x) (CVE-2026-104850, CVSS 3.1 7.5, CWE-345/CWE-522, GHSA-6qxp-vccf-f47h). Only an application that uses the SDK as an MCP client over HTTP with an `authProvider` (its own `OAuthClientProvider`, or the bundled `ClientCredentialsProvider`, `PrivateKeyJwtProvider`, `StaticPrivateKeyJwtProvider` or, on 2.x, `CrossAppAccessProvider`) and may connect to an MCP server it does not fully trust is exposed. 1.31.0 and 2.2.0 record the authorization server as `issuer` on saved credentials and do not send them to another one.
rules.limitations: Reports `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` from 1.12.0 up to 1.31.0 and `@modelcontextprotocol/client` below 2.2.0 where a package.json, lockfile or MCP config states the version, reporting a range that admits an affected version. `latest` and other tags state no version and are not reported. It reads the version, not how the SDK is used, so an MCP server built on the SDK, or a client that speaks only stdio, is reported without being exposed. `@modelcontextprotocol/core` is not read: the advisory names it only as an upgrade for direct importers, and `@modelcontextprotocol/client` 2.2.0 pins it at 2.2.0. A file over 2 MB, or a lockfile over 32 MiB, is not read. A declaration nested more than 64 levels deep in package.json, a TOML manifest or an MCP config (an MCP server more than 62) is still judged, and reported without a line; a lockfile entry keeps its line at any depth.
rules.remediation: Upgrade `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` to 1.31.0 or later, or on 2.x `@modelcontextprotocol/client` (and `@modelcontextprotocol/core`, if you import it directly) to 2.2.0 or later, and pin it. The upgrade alone is not enough: pass `expectedIssuer` to the bundled providers, add `issuer` to credentials saved before the upgrade or clear them, and have your own `OAuthClientProvider` save the `issuer` it is given. Rotate any credential a client may have sent to an MCP server you do not trust.
rules.title: MCP TypeScript SDK 1.12.0 to 1.30.1 (2.x client below 2.2.0): the MCP server picks where OAuth credentials go

rules.description: The official MCP TypeScript SDK (`@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` on npm) ships an experimental tasks feature: a server that passes a `taskStore` to `McpServer` or `Server` lets clients run requests as tasks and poll, list and cancel them later. From 1.24.0, where the feature and its `InMemoryTaskStore` first ship, until 1.32.0, every method of that store took the caller's session id and ignored it, so all clients sharing one store shared one pool of tasks: a client with a session of its own could list the tasks another session created, read their results and cancel them (CVE-2026-111767, CVSS 3.1 8.6, CWE-639/CWE-862, GHSA-22jm-h49p-29qw). 1.32.0 records the session on `createTask`, answers another session's lookup, result read, status update or cancel as a task not found, pages `listTasks` per session, and checks a request's related task against its session before queueing anything for it (modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk#2925). Only an HTTP server that passes `taskStore` is exposed; the 2.x packages (`@modelcontextprotocol/server`, `client` and `core`) are not affected. Experimental tasks are deprecated: the 2026-07-28 specification replaced them with a redesigned extension.
rules.limitations: Reports `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` from 1.24.0 up to 1.32.0 where a package.json, lockfile or MCP config states the version, reporting a range that admits an affected version. `latest` was 1.32.1 on 2026-10-21 and states no version, so it is not reported. It reads the version, not whether a server passes `taskStore`, so a server or client on an affected version that never uses experimental tasks is reported without being exposed; the advisory's own test is that `grep -ri taskstore` outside node_modules finds nothing. 1.23.1, published after 1.24.0, ships no task store and is not reported, and the 2.x packages are not read. A file over 2 MB, or a lockfile over 32 MiB, is not read. A declaration nested more than 64 levels deep in package.json, a TOML manifest or an MCP config (an MCP server more than 62) is still judged, and reported without a line; a lockfile entry keeps its line at any depth.
rules.remediation: Upgrade `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` to 1.32.0 or later and pin it. If you cannot upgrade yet, stop passing `taskStore`, or create one `InMemoryTaskStore` per session. Experimental tasks are deprecated in favour of the 2026-07-28 specification's redesigned extension, so plan to leave them.
rules.title: MCP TypeScript SDK 1.24.0 to 1.31.0: experimental tasks are not tied to the session that created them

rules.description: An MCP Tunnels gateway-proxy config (`/etc/mcp-gateway/config.yaml` or the Helm `gateway.config.*` ConfigMap) either sets `upstream.disable_ip_validation: true` or names an `upstream.allowed_ips` CIDR that covers the public internet (0.0.0.0/0, ::/0, or a /0–/7 IPv4 prefix). The reference page calls `upstream.allowed_ips` the proxy's primary SSRF defense; disabling it lets a malicious upstream-side process reach arbitrary hosts the proxy can route to.
rules.limitations: Fires on `upstream.disable_ip_validation: true`, or an `upstream.allowed_ips` entry that is `0.0.0.0/0` or `::/0` or has an IPv4 prefix of /7 or shorter or an IPv6 prefix of /31 or shorter, in a YAML document with `tunnel_domain` and `routes` at the top (or under `gateway.config`); every document of a multi-document file is read. Only a file named config, proxy or values (.yaml or .yml), or one under a directory named tunnel, gateway, mcp-tunnel, mcp-tunnels, mcp-gateway, mcp_tunnel or mcp_gateway, is read, so the same settings embedded as a string in a Kubernetes ConfigMap's `data:`, or set in a document with no `tunnel_domain` and `routes` of its own (an override layered onto another document), are not seen.
rules.remediation: Set `upstream.allowed_ips` to the smallest CIDR ranges that cover your MCP servers (the reference's default is the RFC1918 private space). Remove `disable_ip_validation: true`. See https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/security (`Restrict upstream.allowed_ips`).
rules.title: MCP Tunnels proxy: SSRF defense disabled or bypassed

rules.description: An MCP Tunnels gateway-proxy config declares one or more `https://` upstreams under `routes:` but sets neither `upstream.tls.ca_file` nor `upstream.tls.include_system_cas: true`. Quoting the reference: "otherwise the proxy has no trust anchor for the upstream certificate." Without a trust anchor the proxy will fail closed at best or accept a man-in-the-middle's certificate at worst, depending on the proxy build.
rules.limitations: Fires on an `https://` route in a proxy config (a YAML file with `tunnel_domain` and `routes`) when neither `upstream.tls.ca_file` nor `upstream.tls.include_system_cas` is set. Only a file named config, proxy or values (.yaml or .yml), or one under a directory named tunnel, gateway, mcp-tunnel, mcp-tunnels, mcp-gateway, mcp_tunnel or mcp_gateway, is read, so the same configuration saved as `deploy/proxy-prod.yaml` is not.
rules.remediation: Add `upstream.tls.ca_file: <path>` pointing at a CA bundle that issued the upstream certificates, OR set `upstream.tls.include_system_cas: true` to trust the system CA bundle. See https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/reference#proxy-configuration.
rules.title: MCP Tunnels proxy: HTTPS upstream without trust anchor

rules.description: A tunnel token or server TLS private key is checked into the repository or pinned as a literal value in a CI workflow. Per the MCP Tunnels overview, "if an attacker obtains your tunnel token AND one of your TLS private keys, they could impersonate your proxy and read MCP request payloads — treat both as high-value secrets." Triggers on literal tunnel-token env vars in CI, PEM private keys committed under MCP-Tunnels paths, and Kubernetes Secret manifests named `mcp-tunnel` / `mcp-tunnel-token` / `mcp-tunnel-cert` carrying inline `data:` values.
rules.limitations: Looks for a literal value for one of a fixed set of token names (`MCP_TUNNEL_TOKEN`, `TUNNEL_TOKEN`, `ANTHROPIC_IDENTITY_TOKEN` and two more) on a `KEY: value` line of a GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Azure Pipelines or CircleCI file, for a PEM private key in a file under a tunnel or gateway directory, and for a Kubernetes Secret named exactly `mcp-tunnel`, `mcp-tunnel-token` or `mcp-tunnel-cert`. The same token in a `docker-compose.yml`, or in a Secret with any other name, is not examined.
rules.remediation: Move tunnel tokens and server-cert material into a secrets manager (GitHub Actions secrets, Vault, sealed-secrets, External Secrets Operator, vault-secrets-operator). For the setup CLI, use Workload Identity Federation (`ANTHROPIC_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE`) instead of a literal token. See https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-tunnels/security (`Protect credentials at rest`, `Rotate credentials`).
rules.title: MCP Tunnels: tunnel credentials hardcoded in repo / CI

rules.description: Microsoft UFO, the open-source framework for intelligent automation across devices and platforms, before 3.0.8 exposes two Streamable-HTTP MCP services from `ufo/client/mcp/http_servers/mobile_mcp_server.py`: `create_mobile_data_collection_server` on TCP 8020 and `create_mobile_action_server` on TCP 8021. Neither applies inbound authentication, so an unauthenticated remote attacker who can reach either port invokes `capture_screenshot`, `get_ui_tree`, `tap`, `swipe`, `type_text`, `launch_app`, `press_key` and `click_control` against the ADB-connected Android device — disclosing screen contents and device data, and modifying device state (CVE-2026-73296, CVSS 9.4). Fixed in 3.0.8. UFO is distributed as a git checkout rather than a PyPI or npm artifact (`ufo` on npm is unjs's unrelated URL library), so this ships as a detection rule rather than a version pin.
rules.limitations: The dependency check reads requirements* files, pyproject.toml, Pipfile, poetry.lock and uv.lock, and recognises a UFO checkout only as an `https://github.com/microsoft/UFO` URL, unpinned or below 3.0.8. The same checkout installed from a Dockerfile (`RUN pip install git+https://github.com/microsoft/UFO.git`) or referenced over SSH (`git+ssh://git@github.com/microsoft/UFO.git@v3.0.2`) is not matched.
rules.remediation: Upgrade UFO to >= 3.0.8. Bind the mobile data-collection and mobile action MCP servers to 127.0.0.1 rather than all interfaces, and require an inbound credential on both. Do not expose an ADB-connected device's MCP control surface to any untrusted network.
rules.title: Microsoft UFO < 3.0.8 (mobile MCP servers on 8020/8021 with no authentication)

rules.description: Uni-CLI (`@zenalexa/unicli` on npm; olo-dot-io/Uni-CLI) gives people and agents one command interface for websites, browsers, desktop applications, local tools and MCP, and can serve MCP over HTTP on loopback. Before 0.225.2 its legacy JSON-RPC-over-HTTP transport routed requests without checking the browser's `Origin`, so a web page could send a CORS-simple `POST` (`text/plain`) to the local `/mcp` endpoint and drive `tools/call` against the user's Uni-CLI server once that transport was started (CVE-2026-58497, CVSS 4.0 8.6, CWE-346/CWE-352, GHSA-v3f4-w7r7-v3hm). The Streamable HTTP transport already enforced that browser-to-localhost boundary; the legacy path had drifted from it. 0.225.2 routes every request on both transports through one `isOriginAllowed` guard. The flaw is the browser-to-localhost boundary, not Uni-CLI's local-code-execution trust model.
rules.limitations: Reports `@zenalexa/unicli` from 0.208.0 below 0.225.2 where a package.json, lockfile or MCP config states the version, reporting a range that admits an affected version. 0.207.1, the first release, has no HTTP transport and is not reported. `latest` was 1.3.0 on 2026-10-24 and states no version, so an unversioned reference is not reported. It reads the version, not which transport runs, so a server only ever started over stdio is reported too. npm's `uni-cli` is another project and is not matched. A file over 2 MB, or a lockfile over 32 MiB, is not read. A declaration nested more than 64 levels deep in package.json, a TOML manifest or an MCP config (an MCP server more than 62) is still judged, and reported without a line; a lockfile entry keeps its line at any depth.
rules.remediation: Upgrade `@zenalexa/unicli` to 0.225.2 or later and pin it. Until then serve MCP over stdio, or over the Streamable HTTP transport, which checked `Origin` before 0.225.2 too.
rules.title: Uni-CLI from 0.208.0 below 0.225.2: the legacy HTTP MCP transport answers a web page's request to loopback /mcp

rules.description: Unla (AmoyLab/Unla, formerly mcp-gateway) is a Go MCP gateway that ships as container images: `ghcr.io/amoylab/unla/allinone`, `ghcr.io/amoylab/unla/mcp-gateway`, and the Aliyun mirror `registry.ap-southeast-1.aliyuncs.com/amoylab/unla-allinone` its Chinese README names. Its built-in OAuth2 server never authenticates a resource owner: `/authorize` issues a code to any registered client without asking who the user is, and `/token` exchanges it. So an unauthenticated attacker can register a client, get a code and exchange it for a valid access token, which opens the OAuth2-protected MCP prefixes, the upstream APIs Unla proxies and the credentials it injects into them (CVE-2026-108865, CVSS 3.1 8.2, CWE-287). The OAuth2 server arrived in v0.6.0, the `amoylab/unla` images start at v0.7.0, and v0.10.0, the newest release, still issues codes this way. `internal/auth/oauth.go` has not changed since 2025-10-11, so there is no fixed release.
rules.limitations: Reads the three Unla image names in compose files, Kubernetes manifests, Helm values, Dockerfiles and MCP configs, up to and including v0.10.0, and `latest`, which was the v0.10.0 digest on 2026-10-13. The `main` tag and commit tags state no version and are not reported, and images from before the rename (`mcp-ecosystem/mcp-gateway`) are not read. The pin reads the image tag, not the gateway's configuration, so an instance with no OAuth2-protected MCP prefix is reported too.
rules.remediation: There is no fixed release. Put an authenticating reverse proxy in front of Unla's `/authorize`, `/token` and its OAuth2-protected MCP prefixes, and keep the gateway off untrusted networks. If an instance was reachable, rotate the upstream credentials it injects. Pin the first fixed release once it ships.
rules.title: Unla gateway image through v0.10.0: the built-in OAuth2 server issues tokens without authenticating anyone (no fixed release)

rules.description: `utcp-mcp` (PyPI), the MCP plugin of python-utcp, connects to the HTTP and WebSocket MCP server URLs in a call template's `mcpServers` configuration. Before 1.1.3 it dialed them as configured, without the HTTPS/WSS-or-loopback check the HTTP-family plugins apply, so a template naming a plain-HTTP, non-loopback server sends the MCP handshake in cleartext, open to interception, and can reach internal hosts (CVE-2026-101057, CVSS 3.1 3.1, CWE-319). The configuration is operator-authored, which limits practical exploitation. 1.1.3 adds `_ensure_secure_mcp_url` and runs it on every server URL before any connection.
rules.limitations: Reports a reference that names the PyPI package `utcp-mcp` below 1.1.3: a requirements, pyproject or lockfile entry, or the package in an MCP config, where an unpinned reference is reported. It reads the version, not the call template. `AAK-TRANSPORT-001`, which flags an `http://` MCP server URL, reads a top-level `mcpServers`, and utcp nests it under the template's `config` or passes it inline from Python, so a plain-HTTP URL in a template is not reported on its own. A file over 2 MB, or a lockfile over 32 MiB, is not read. A declaration nested more than 64 levels deep in package.json, a TOML manifest or an MCP config (an MCP server more than 62) is still judged, and reported without a line; a lockfile entry keeps its line at any depth.
rules.remediation: Upgrade `utcp-mcp` to 1.1.3 or later and pin it, and use `https://` or `wss://` for any MCP server that is not on loopback.
rules.title: utcp-mcp below 1.1.3 dials plain-HTTP MCP server URLs from a call template

rules.description: `voice-mode` (PyPI; mbailey/voicemode), a voice MCP server, lets its `update_config` MCP tool (and `voicemode config set`) write a caller-supplied value into `~/.voicemode/voicemode.env`. Before 8.10.2 a value with a space or a quote was wrapped in double quotes and anything else written as is, and the service start scripts `source` that file, so `$(...)` or backticks in the value run as shell commands the next time the service starts (CVE-2026-79535, CVSS 3.1 6.3, CWE-78, GHSA-h97v-r3jw-cf6f). 8.10.2 writes only shell-inert values bare and single-quotes everything else (fix commit `c1cef853`).
rules.limitations: Reports a reference that names the PyPI package: a requirements, pyproject or lockfile entry, or `voice-mode` in an MCP config, where an unpinned `uvx voice-mode` is reported as unpinned, as for the other PyPI pins. It reads versions, not the env file: a value written by an older release stays in `voicemode.env` after the upgrade. A file over 2 MB, or a lockfile over 32 MiB, is not read. A declaration nested more than 64 levels deep in package.json, a TOML manifest or an MCP config (an MCP server more than 62) is still judged, and reported without a line; a lockfile entry keeps its line at any depth.
rules.remediation: Upgrade `voice-mode` to 8.10.2 or later and pin it. Check `~/.voicemode/voicemode.env` for values containing `$(`, backticks or `;` written before the upgrade.
rules.title: VoiceMode below 8.10.2 writes MCP-supplied config values into a sourced env file unescaped

rules.description: The WhatsApp MCP Server's `whatsapp-bridge` HTTP API before 0.2.1 listens on 127.0.0.1:8080 with no authentication and no Host-header validation, and its `/api/send` endpoint accepts an absolute `media_path` with no directory confinement. Any local process running as the same user — which in an MCP session includes sibling MCP servers, IDE extensions, and tool-triggered flows — can send WhatsApp messages from the paired account and read then exfiltrate arbitrary user-readable files (SSH keys, browser session data, dotfiles) as document attachments; the missing Host validation also enables DNS-rebinding from a visited webpage (CVE-2026-46555, CVSS 7.7). Fixed in 0.2.1, which adds required bearer-token auth, a Host allow-list, and media_path confinement. The project is the GitHub repository verygoodplugins/whatsapp-mcp, which ships as a clone and release assets and on no registry; npm's and PyPI's `whatsapp-mcp` are other projects. A reference to the repository that names an earlier release is reported.
rules.limitations: Reads a reference to `github.com/verygoodplugins/whatsapp-mcp` that names a release below v0.2.1: a git URL with `@v0.2.0` or `@refs/tags/v0.2.0`, a lockfile's git source with `rev=` or `tag=`, a `/releases/download/` asset or an `/archive/` tarball, and a `tag`, `rev`, `ref` or `reference` key beside a `git` or `url` key that names the repository (uv sources, Poetry, Pipfile, poetry.lock). It reads requirements*.txt, `*.mcp.yaml` and `*.mcp.yml` at any depth and, at the project root only, pyproject.toml, Pipfile, package.json, .mcp.json, mcp.json, claude_desktop_config.json and the Pipfile.lock, poetry.lock, uv.lock, package-lock.json, pnpm-lock.yaml and yarn.lock lockfiles. The install the project's README documents, a clone run with `uv --directory <path> run main.py`, states no version and is not reported, and neither is a reference by commit or branch, or one in `.cursor/mcp.json`, `.vscode/mcp.json`, a sub-directory manifest (`services/api/pyproject.toml`) or `pdm.lock`. npm's and PyPI's `whatsapp-mcp`, and PyPI's `whatsapp-mcp-server`, are other projects and are not read. A file over 2 MB, or a lockfile over 32 MiB, is not read.
rules.remediation: Update the verygoodplugins/whatsapp-mcp checkout or release to v0.2.1 or later and pin that tag, then restart both the bridge and the MCP server so the server reads the bridge token. Require the bridge bearer token on all requests, enable Host-header allow-listing, and confine `media_path` to a configured root (reject absolute paths and `..`). Do not run the bridge next to untrusted local MCP servers, browser extensions, or other untrusted processes.
rules.title: WhatsApp MCP (verygoodplugins/whatsapp-mcp) below 0.2.1 (unauthenticated loopback bridge + media_path traversal → file exfil)

rules.description: ZCode, Z.ai's coding agent (a desktop client and a `zcode` CLI built from one source tree), reads MCP servers from a workspace's `zcode.json` and `.zcode/config.json`, under `mcp.servers`, in every directory from the git root down to the folder it opens, and connects every one at session start without asking. A stdio server's `command` runs as the user the moment the repository is opened, and each server's tool descriptions enter the agent's context (CVE-2026-88755, CWE-284/CWE-863). ZCode's own configuration guide says workspace servers "were previously untrusted and required manual authorization; they now connect by default like any other scope". NVD names 3.11.2.6792. Checked in the source: 3.14.0 (2026-09-20), 3.14.3 and 3.15.1 (2026-10-10), every published release, keep the set of untrusted project servers empty in `runtime-config.ts`, under a comment that project-scoped MCP is trusted by default and connects automatically, so there is no fixed release.
rules.limitations: Reports each ZCode workspace file once, naming every server ZCode would start; whether a server is hostile is for the MCP config rules, which read the same servers. ZCode ships as desktop installers and an install script, so its version is in no file AAK reads, and every such file with an enabled server is reported, whatever release opens it. A server is not re-checked against ZCode's schema, which drops an entry with an unknown key, so that entry is still named. A file that is not strict JSON is skipped, as ZCode skips it. The desktop client falls back to `.agents/mcp.json` at the workspace root when `.zcode/config.json` declares no server; other agents read that file too, and it is not reported here.
rules.remediation: Read a repository's `zcode.json` and `.zcode/config.json` before opening it in ZCode: its guide offers no way to have it ask first. In your own project, keep personal servers in `~/.zcode/cli/config.json` rather than the workspace file, or set `"enabled": false` on a workspace server so ZCode skips it.
rules.title: ZCode connects the MCP servers a workspace's config declares when the folder is opened, without approval

rules.description: `zscaler-mcp` (PyPI; zscaler/zscaler-mcp-server) asks for confirmation before a write tool runs: the first call returns an HMAC token signed over the tool name and its arguments, and the second call must present it. In 0.7.0 and 0.7.1, 31 delete tools across ZIA, ZPA and ZTW passed an empty parameter set to `check_confirmation()`, so the token named no resource, and a token issued to delete one resource confirmed the delete of any other of the same type within its five-minute lifetime (CVE-2026-59563, CVSS 3.1 4.6, CWE-305). An agent given one confirmation could spend it on a resource nobody confirmed. 0.6.2 bound the arguments on every call, and 0.7.2 passes each resource id into the token (zscaler/zscaler-mcp-server#41).
rules.limitations: Reports a reference that names the PyPI package `zscaler-mcp` at 0.7.0 or 0.7.1: a requirements, pyproject or lockfile entry, or the package in an MCP config, where an unpinned `uvx zscaler-mcp` is reported as unpinned, as for the other PyPI pins. `zscaler-mcp-server`, the name in the README's uvx example, is not a PyPI package and is not read. The Docker Hub image has no tag below 0.12, so there is no image to pin. A file over 2 MB, or a lockfile over 32 MiB, is not read. A declaration nested more than 64 levels deep in package.json, a TOML manifest or an MCP config (an MCP server more than 62) is still judged, and reported without a line; a lockfile entry keeps its line at any depth.
rules.remediation: Upgrade `zscaler-mcp` to 0.7.2 or later and pin it.
rules.title: Zscaler MCP Server 0.7.0 and 0.7.1: delete confirmation tokens are not bound to the resource

rules.description: The PyPI package `mcp-calculate-server` <0.1.1 has a remote code execution vulnerability in its MCP tool handler — the math expression is routed through `eval()` (SymPy-backed without `local_dict` / `global_dict` namespace pinning), so an attacker controlling the tool input reaches host RCE. CVE-2026-44717 (CVSS 9.8 CRITICAL, NVD 2026-05-15). Patched in 0.1.1 (latest at AAK ship time: 1.0.0). This pin-only rule fires on the package in any Python manifest (`requirements*.txt`, `pyproject.toml`, `Pipfile*`, `poetry.lock`, `uv.lock`). A broader source-detector for the unsafe-`eval()` shape inside any `@tool` / `@mcp.tool()` decorated handler is queued for v0.3.19+ — it would catch single-author MCP servers with the same shape, not just this product.
rules.limitations: Matches `mcp-calculate-server` followed directly by a version (`mcp-calculate-server==0.1.0`) in requirements*.txt at the project root and in a dependency string of the root pyproject.toml. A name with no version, a git URL, the table form that Poetry and Pipfile use (`mcp-calculate-server = "^0.1.0"`), a requirements file in a sub-directory and an `.mcp.json` launcher are not reported. Pipfile.lock, poetry.lock and uv.lock are opened but never match, because the name and the version sit on separate lines, so a version that reaches the project only through a lockfile is not reported. A file over 2 MB, or a lockfile over 32 MiB, is not read.
rules.remediation: Bump `mcp-calculate-server` to >= 0.1.1 (or the latest 1.x). If you maintain a similar MCP server, replace `eval()` with `ast.literal_eval` for plain numerics, or SymPy `parse_expr(expr, local_dict={}, global_dict={}, evaluate=True)` with explicit allow-listed symbol tables.
rules.title: MCP Calculate Server eval() RCE (CVE-2026-44717, PyPI <0.1.1)

rules.description: Project depends on `mcp-framework` at a version < 0.2.22, or a TS/JS file implements an MCP HTTP transport that concatenates request body chunks into a string without consulting Content-Length or a `maxMessageSize` guard. CVE-2026-39313 lets an unauthenticated attacker crash the server with a single large POST to /mcp by exhausting process memory. Fixed in 0.2.22.
rules.limitations: Fires on a TypeScript or JavaScript file that reads a request body with `req.on('data', ...)`, `for await (... of req)` or a function called `readRequestBody` and appends chunks to a variable named body, data, buf or chunks (a leading underscore allowed, as in `this._body`), with `+=` of a name or of its `.toString(...)`, or with `.push(chunk)`, in code rather than a comment, and has no size check. A comparison with `<`, `>`, `<=` or `>=` of total, length or size against a number literal anywhere in the file, such as `parts.length > 0`, counts as a size check, and an accumulator under another name (`raw += chunk`) is not matched. A `req.on('data', ...)` whose first `)` comes more than 1,024 characters after the comma, as behind a long comment in the handler, is not read as a body read; on 88,502 TS/JS files it came at most 36 after. The version pin judges a git reference, a tarball and a `workspace:` spec by the release they name, with releases compared on their first three numbers, so a pre-release of the fix (`#v0.2.22-rc.1`) reads as the fix, and it does not read a `package.json` over 2 MB. A source file over 512 KB is not read.
rules.remediation: Upgrade `mcp-framework` to 0.2.22 or newer. For custom transports, enforce a hard body-size cap before accumulating chunks — reject early when `Content-Length` exceeds your `maxMessageSize`.
rules.title: mcp-framework < 0.2.22 HTTP-body DoS

rules.description: Two routes matching the MCP endpoint pattern (`/mcp`, `/mcp_message`, `/mcp/messages`, `/mcp[_-]invoke`, `/mcp[_-]tool`, ...) are declared in the same file, but one has no auth middleware while its twin does. This is the exact CVE-2026-33032 shape nginx-ui 2.3.4 patched and which VulnCheck KEV-listed on 2026-04-13 as actively exploited (CVSS 9.8). ~2,689 Shodan instances were exposed at disclosure; any network-adjacent caller can invoke the protected tools with zero credentials.
rules.limitations: Compares MCP routes inside one file: it fires on an unauthenticated route (`/mcp`, `/mcp_message`, `/mcp-messages`, `/mcp/invoke` and a few more) only when another MCP route in the same file has an auth marker from a fixed list. Twin routes placed in two modules are not paired, a path such as `/mcp/sse` is not recognised as an MCP route, an auth dependency that is not on the list (`Depends(verify_api_key)`) does not count as auth, and a FastAPI route written with single quotes (`@router.post('/mcp')`) is not read. A Gin or Express route's middleware arguments are read for auth markers in their first 200 characters, and its handler up to its first `)` within 200; in TypeScript and JavaScript a regex literal must close within 512 characters of its `/`, or it is read as division and a backtick in it can hide the routes after it.
rules.remediation: Apply the same auth middleware to every MCP endpoint in a file. For Gin, use a `router.Use(AuthRequired())` group and mount all MCP routes inside it. For FastAPI, share a single `Depends(auth)` dependency across `@app.post('/mcp*')` decorators. For Express, create an `mcpRouter.use(authMw)` and mount it once.
rules.title: MCP route twin-asymmetry: auth middleware missing on sibling route (MCPwn, CVE-2026-33032)

rules.description: `meta-ads-mcp` before 1.0.109 has `AuthInjectionMiddleware.dispatch()` unconditionally forward unauthenticated Streamable-HTTP requests to downstream MCP tool handlers without a 401, so any network-reachable caller invokes tools unauthenticated. With no per-request credential the handlers fall back to the `META_ACCESS_TOKEN` env var, and when the downstream Meta Graph API call fails the raw `httpx` request URL — including the operator's `access_token` query parameter — is serialised into the JSON-RPC response, delivering the credential to the unauthenticated caller (CVE-2026-48039, CVSS 9.1). Fixed in 1.0.109; treat < 1.0.109 (and unpinned) as exposed.
rules.limitations: Reads `meta-ads-mcp` in requirements*.txt at any depth and, at the project root only, in pyproject.toml, Pipfile, .mcp.json, mcp.json, claude_desktop_config.json and the Pipfile.lock, poetry.lock and uv.lock lockfiles, taking the lowest version a range allows and reporting a reference that states no version. The dependency is not read when it is declared in a sub-directory manifest (`services/api/pyproject.toml`), in `.cursor/mcp.json` or `.vscode/mcp.json`, or in a lockfile format the reader does not parse (`pdm.lock`). A file over 2 MB, or a lockfile over 32 MiB, is not read. A declaration nested more than 64 levels deep in package.json, a TOML manifest or an MCP config (an MCP server more than 62) is still judged, and reported without a line; a lockfile entry keeps its line at any depth.
rules.remediation: Upgrade `meta-ads-mcp` to >= 1.0.109 and pin it. Require per-request authentication and return 401 when it is absent; never echo an outbound request URL (which carries `access_token`) into a tool response, and scrub credentials from error paths.
rules.title: Meta Ads MCP forwards unauthenticated requests and leaks the access token (< 1.0.109)

rules.description: A function consumes an LLM-refusal signal (parameter name or local variable matches `refusal`/`rejected`/`denied`/`decline`/`handle_refusal`) and either (a) returns the refusal value or (b) passes it as an argument to a prompt-sink call (`format` / `append` / `add_message` / `build_prompt` / etc.) without first re-categorizing it into an opaque token. Per *Metis: Learning to Jailbreak LLMs via Self-Evolving Metacognitive Policy Optimization* (arXiv:2605.10067, ICML 2026), structured refusal feedback used as a semantic gradient is the exploited surface. **Research-grade — MEDIUM severity reflects non-trivial false-positive risk; treat as a code-review prompt, not an automatic block.**
rules.limitations: Follows a refusal only through a parameter or variable whose name contains `refusal`, `rejected`, `denied`, `denial` or `decline` (and plain copies of it), and reports it only when it is returned or passed as a bare argument to `append`, `extend`, `format`, `add_message` and the other listed sink calls. Wrapped in a dict or an f-string (`messages.append({"role": "user", "content": refusal})`) it is not reported, and a variable called `refused` is never tracked. A Python file over 512 KB is not read.
rules.remediation: Wrap the refusal value in a policy-mediated transformation before re-use: discretize into a fixed enum (e.g., `RefusalKind.POLICY` / `RefusalKind.SAFETY`), rate-limit retries, strip free-text content. Never echo a verbatim refusal sentence into the next prompt — that is the closed-loop reasoning gradient Metis exploits.
rules.title: Refusal text re-fed into prompt without policy mediation (Metis, research-grade)

rules.description: A function consumes a scoring / judge signal (parameter or local variable matches `score`/`scoring`/`judge`/`reward`/`rating`/`critique`) and passes it into a prompt-sink call (`format` / `append` / `add_message` / `build_prompt` / etc.) without discretizing the signal first. Per Metis (arXiv:2605.10067), numeric or verbose scoring strings are exactly the semantic gradient an adversary uses to refine its policy across closed-loop reasoning iterations. **Research-grade — MEDIUM severity reflects non-trivial false-positive risk.**
rules.limitations: Follows a score only through a parameter or variable whose name contains `score`, `judge`, `reward`, `rating` or `critique` (and plain copies of it), and reports it only when it is passed as a bare argument to a call named `format`, `append`, `extend`, `add_message`, `build_prompt` and the like. Putting it into an f-string (`f"Your last draft scored {score}"`), or into a dict passed to `append`, is not reported. A Python file over 512 KB is not read.
rules.remediation: Discretize scoring signals into an opaque bucket (e.g., PASS / FAIL / PARTIAL) before re-injecting. If a numeric score must be exposed, cap it (e.g., 0-3 ordinal) and avoid free-text critiques. Per Metis: any verbose feedback string is fuel for the metacognitive policy refinement the paper demonstrates.
rules.title: Scoring / judge value flows into prompt-sink call (Metis, research-grade)

rules.description: A dependency pin targets mcp-neo4j-cypher earlier than 0.6.0, or source code sets read_only=True while issuing CALL apoc.* / db.cypher.runWrite procedures. CVE-2026-35402 (CVSS 2.3 LOW, but integrity-critical) lets attackers bypass the read-only mode and execute arbitrary writes or SSRF.
rules.limitations: The pin reads requirements.txt, requirements-dev.txt, requirements-prod.txt, dev-requirements.txt and pyproject.toml at the project root, taking the lowest version a range allows. A git reference or an archive is judged by the release its tag or file name names, with releases compared on their first three numbers, so a pre-release of the fix (`v0.6.0-rc1`) reads as the fix. An unpinned line, a git reference to a commit or a branch included (any name holding a `/` but `refs/tags/<tag>`), is not reported, and uv.lock, `requirements/base.txt` and a `uvx mcp-neo4j-cypher==0.5.0 --read-only` launcher in .mcp.json are not read, nor is a pyproject.toml that does not parse or a manifest over 2 MB. A pyproject.toml with a key of more than 64 dotted parts, or holding an integer Python cannot convert (one past 4,300 digits), is refused and reported as AAK-INTERNAL-SCANNER-FAIL. Declarations of one install that no release satisfies together (`mcp-neo4j-cypher==0.6.0` beside `mcp-neo4j-cypher==0.5.0` in one requirements file) admit nothing and are not reported; pip refuses to install them too. The source arm needs `read_only = True` and a `CALL apoc.` or `runWrite` reference in the same Python file, so a query kept in another module is not matched. A requirements file over 2 MB is not read.
rules.remediation: Upgrade mcp-neo4j-cypher to 0.6.0 or later. In source code, stop relying on read_only=True as a security boundary when APOC procedures are in scope; deny-list apoc.* at the query layer.
rules.title: mcp-neo4j-cypher < 0.6.0 APOC read-only bypass

rules.description: Project depends on `next-ai-draw-io` at a version below 0.4.15. CVE-2026-40608 is a body-accumulation OOM in the embedded HTTP sidecar's /api/state, /api/restore and /api/history-svg handlers — the entire request body is concatenated into a JavaScript string without a size cap, so a single ~500 MiB POST exhausts V8 heap and crashes the MCP server. Same DoS class as AAK-MCPFRAME-001. Fixed in 0.4.15.
rules.limitations: Reads the dependency maps and overrides of the `package.json` at the root of the scanned directory, taking the lowest version a range allows and reporting a reference that states no version, such as a git reference to a commit or a branch (any name holding a `/` but `refs/tags/<tag>`). A git reference, a tarball and a `workspace:` spec are judged by the release they name, with releases compared on their first three numbers, so a pre-release of the fix (`#v0.4.15-rc.1`) reads as the fix. The same dependency declared in a workspace package's own `package.json` (`apps/web/package.json`) is not read, and neither is a `package.json` over 2 MB. A source file over 512 KB is not read.
rules.remediation: Upgrade `next-ai-draw-io` to 0.4.15 or later. For custom transports that replicate the pattern, enforce a hard body-size cap before accumulating chunks and reject early when `Content-Length` exceeds the cap.
rules.title: next-ai-draw-io < 0.4.15 body-accumulation DoS

rules.description: An OAuth 2.1 client flow does not use PKCE. PKCE is mandatory for all MCP remote server clients per spec 2025-11-25, including confidential clients.
rules.limitations: Fires on a call to `authorize(` or the name `authorization_endpoint` in a file that has no whole word `code_verifier` or `pkce` and no `code_challenge` outside `code_challenge_method`. An authorization URL written out as a literal (`https://auth.example.com/authorize?response_type=code`) is not recognised as an authorization request.
rules.remediation: Add a code_verifier/code_challenge pair to every authorization request. Use code_challenge_method=S256.
rules.title: OAuth flow without PKCE

rules.description: An OAuth client sets code_challenge_method=plain. S256 is mandatory; 'plain' leaks the verifier to anyone with access to the authorization request.
rules.limitations: Examines only files that contain a word starting with oauth, authorization_endpoint, token_endpoint or client_id (in any case; `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID` does not count) or the call `authorize(`. In them it fires only when `code_challenge_method` is assigned the literal `plain` (`code_challenge_method=plain`, `"code_challenge_method": "plain"`). An authorization request that sends `code_challenge` with no `code_challenge_method` defaults to `plain` (RFC 7636 §4.3) and is not reported. Neither is a method taken from a constant (`METHOD = "plain"`), or the same literal in a file with none of those words.
rules.remediation: Set code_challenge_method=S256 and derive code_challenge as BASE64URL(SHA256(code_verifier)).
rules.title: PKCE using the plain challenge method

rules.description: An MCP server receives a bearer token from one identity and forwards it to a downstream service without re-minting. This is the 'confused deputy' shape banned by OAuth 2.1 BCPs.
rules.limitations: Examines only files that contain a word starting with oauth, authorization_endpoint, token_endpoint or client_id (in any case; `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID` does not count) or the call `authorize(`. In them it matches a dict entry `"Authorization": request.headers[...]` (quoted key, header read by subscript; also req, event, input) and any assignment `headers["Authorization"] = request....`. A dict entry read with `.get` or as a property (`req.headers.authorization`), one with an unquoted key (`{ Authorization: req.headers["authorization"] }`), and the same forwarding in a file with none of those words, are not matched.
rules.remediation: Use token-exchange (RFC 8693) or a service account to call downstream services. Never forward a user token across trust boundaries.
rules.title: OAuth token passthrough between tenants

rules.description: An OAuth client registers a wildcard, localhost-with-any-port, or overly-broad redirect_uri. Attackers can hijack authorization codes via dangling subdomains or open redirectors.
rules.limitations: Examines only files that contain a word starting with oauth, authorization_endpoint, token_endpoint or client_id (in any case; `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID` does not count) or the call `authorize(`. In them it matches a `redirect_uri` or `redirect_uris` value of `*` or `["*"]`, one that begins with `https://*` or `http://*`, or one that begins with `http://localhost`. A wildcard URL inside a list (`["https://*.example.com/callback"]`), a trailing wildcard (`"https://app.example.com/*"`) and a file with none of those words are not matched.
rules.remediation: Register exact-match redirect URIs only. No wildcards.
rules.title: Wildcard or overly-broad redirect_uri

rules.description: An MCP remote server accepts plain Bearer tokens on a flow that MCP spec 2025-11-25 flags for DPoP (Demonstrating Proof of Possession) or mTLS-bound tokens. A stolen Bearer token is fully replayable.
rules.limitations: Examines only files that contain a word starting with oauth, authorization_endpoint, token_endpoint or client_id (in any case; `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID` does not count) or the call `authorize(`. In them it matches a literal `Bearer <token>` string in a file that also contains `Authorization` and neither `DPoP` nor `cnf`. A token attached the usual way, from a variable (`f"Bearer {token}"`), and the same literal in a file with none of those words, are not matched.
rules.remediation: Require DPoP proofs or mTLS-bound tokens for high-privilege flows. Validate the token's cnf claim.
rules.title: Bearer token used where DPoP or mTLS is required

rules.description: An OAuth authorization-code client processes the authorization response / redirect callback (reads `code` and `state`, or exchanges the code at the token endpoint) but never references the `iss` parameter. The MCP ratified 2026-07-28 spec (SEP-2468) requires clients to validate `iss` on authorization responses per RFC 9207 — without it, an attacker who controls one authorization server in MCP's single-client / many-server deployment can mount an OAuth mix-up attack and have the client redeem a code at the wrong server. This is the token-issuer-validation arm of the 2026-07-28 final MCP auth profile (scanned together with RFC 8707 resource indicators, `AAK-OAUTH-007`, and RFC 9728 Protected-Resource-Metadata discovery, `AAK-OAUTH-008`, via `--profile mcp-2026-07-28`). A later spec version will require rejecting responses that omit `iss` entirely.
rules.limitations: Examines only files that contain a word starting with oauth, authorization_endpoint, token_endpoint or client_id (in any case; `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID` does not count) or the call `authorize(`. In them it fires on a code exchange (`grant_type=authorization_code`, `exchange_code_for_token`, or a read of `code` from the query arguments) when the word `iss` appears nowhere in the file. Any `iss` counts as validating the authorization response, including a JWT claim check on the ID token (`claims["iss"]`), and the same exchange in a file with none of those words is not reported.
rules.remediation: Validate the `iss` authorization-response parameter against the expected issuer of the authorization server the request was sent to (RFC 9207), and reject the response on mismatch. Have your authorization server emit `iss` now so the check can be enforced before the 2026-07-28 cutover.
rules.title: OAuth client does not validate the `iss` authorization-response parameter (RFC 9207)

rules.description: An OAuth 2.1 authorization/token flow — or an MCP client/server config that advertises OAuth 2.1 — builds authorization and/or token requests without the RFC 8707 `resource` parameter. The ratified MCP 2025-11-25 authorization spec requires MCP clients to send `resource` on both the authorization request and the token request, identifying the MCP server by its canonical URI, so the authorization server audience-binds the issued token. Without Resource Indicators the token is not bound to a specific MCP server, so a token minted for one server can be replayed at another (token replay / audience confusion) — the confused-deputy class OAuth 2.1 §5.2 and the MCP spec's Access Token Privilege Restriction section forbid.
rules.limitations: Examines only files that contain a word starting with oauth, authorization_endpoint, token_endpoint or client_id (in any case; `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID` does not count) or the call `authorize(`. In them it fires on a token request (`grant_type=...`, `response_type=code`, `authorize(`, `authorization_endpoint`, `token_endpoint` or an `/authorize` or `/token` path) in a file with no `resource` parameter. In a .json, .yaml, .yml or .toml file the request has to be data: a `grant_type`, `authorization_endpoint` or `token_endpoint` key, `response_type: code`, or a value that is wholly a URL or path ending in `/authorize` or `/token`, so a token path written inside a sentence there is not one. Any `resource = ...` assignment, `"resource":` key, `?resource=` or `&resource=` parameter, `resource_indicator(s)` or the text `RFC 8707` (any case, a comment included) counts as the RFC 8707 parameter, including an unrelated local variable named `resource`, and the same request in a file with none of those words is not reported.
rules.remediation: Set the `resource` parameter to the MCP server's canonical URI so issued tokens are audience-bound (RFC 8707, on both the authorization and token requests); reject tokens whose audience is not this server (validate the audience per RFC 8707 §2 / RFC 9728 §7.4).
rules.title: OAuth flow does not set the RFC 8707 `resource` parameter (Resource Indicators)

rules.description: A remote MCP OAuth surface presents no RFC 9728 Protected Resource Metadata discovery: a client config points at a remote (HTTP/SSE) MCP server and carries an inline / static credential (an `Authorization` / `Bearer` header, an `auth` block, or an embedded token) with no reference to `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource`, `authorization_servers`, or `resource_metadata`; or MCP server source enforces bearer auth (e.g. `WWW-Authenticate`, a FastMCP `BearerAuthProvider`) without serving Protected Resource Metadata. The ratified MCP 2025-11-25 auth spec requires servers to implement RFC 9728 so clients can discover the authorization server and obtain an audience-bound token instead of relying on a pre-shared secret; the 2026-07-28 final auth profile builds on it. Without PRM the deployment cannot participate in discovery-based auth and typically hardcodes credentials.
rules.limitations: Fires on a config with double-quoted keys that declares a remote server (`"type"` or `"transport"` set to http, sse, streamable, streamablehttp or streamable-http, or a `"url"` starting `http://` or `https://`) and carries an inline credential (an `"Authorization":` header, a `Bearer` value, an `"auth": {` block, or an `access_token`, `api_key` or `token` field), or on source that mentions `WWW-Authenticate`, `BearerAuthProvider`, `RequireAuthMiddleware` or `require_auth`, when the file never mentions `oauth-protected-resource`, `protected_resource_metadata` (also with `-` or no separator), `resource_metadata`, `authorization_servers` or `RFC 9728`. A static key in another header (`X-API-Key`) is not recognised as an inline credential, and a config with unquoted keys (YAML `type: http`) is not recognised as a remote server.
rules.remediation: Serve RFC 9728 Protected Resource Metadata at `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` (with an `authorization_servers` entry) and have clients discover the authorization server from it — via the `resource_metadata` field of a 401 `WWW-Authenticate` challenge — instead of embedding a static bearer/token credential in the MCP client config.
rules.title: MCP OAuth surface with no RFC 9728 Protected Resource Metadata discovery

rules.description: The project depends on an agent-platform SDK (context-ai, langsmith, helicone, langfuse, humanloop, MCP SDK). Informational finding so reviewers audit the vendor's OAuth-scope footprint before merging. Raised to MEDIUM because the April 19 2026 Vercel × Context.ai incident showed a single vendor compromise can turn into a production breach via transitive OAuth grants.
rules.limitations: Reads the dependency names of the root package.json (`dependencies`, `devDependencies`, `peerDependencies`), the `[project].dependencies` of the root pyproject.toml and the root requirements*.txt, and matches each name exactly against a fixed list (context-ai, langsmith, helicone, langfuse, humanloop, `@langchain/langsmith`, `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` and the Python mcp, langsmith-py and helicone-py). A requirement with extras (`mcp[cli]>=1.2.0`), another capitalisation (`Langfuse`), `[project.optional-dependencies]` or Poetry tables, a lockfile and a sub-directory manifest are not reported. A package.json or pyproject.toml over 2 MB is not read. A pyproject.toml with a key of more than 64 dotted parts, or holding an integer Python cannot convert (one past 4,300 digits), is refused and reported as AAK-INTERNAL-SCANNER-FAIL.
rules.remediation: Pin the SDK to an exact version, audit the OAuth scopes it requests, and keep any deployment-level grants (Vercel, GCP, Workspace) in a secrets vault — never in a committed env file. See Vercel's bulletin for sensitive-env-var guidance: https://vercel.com/kb/bulletin/vercel-april-2026-security-incident
rules.title: Repo depends on a third-party agent-platform SDK

rules.description: A config file in this repo grants a non-first-party Google OAuth client broad Workspace scopes (admin.*, cloud-platform, drive, directory.*, gmail.modify/send). The April 19 2026 Vercel × Context.ai breach is the template: a single compromised third-party OAuth app with deployment-level scopes let attackers pivot into production. Explicitly allowlist trusted client IDs in `.aak-oauth-trust.yml`.
rules.limitations: Reads a fixed set of paths under the project root (`app.yaml`, `vercel.json`, `netlify.toml`, `oauth.json`, `oauth_client.json`, `client_secret*.json`, `.well-known/oauth-client-credentials.json` and `.google-cloud-sdk/**/*.json`) for Google scopes under admin.*, cloud-platform, drive, gmail.modify, gmail.send and directory.*. Scopes written in source code (`SCOPES = [...]` in a `.py` file) and `https://mail.google.com/` are not matched. A config file over 1 MB is not read.
rules.remediation: Review the granted scopes — drop admin.* / cloud-platform where possible. Add every legitimate third-party client_id to `.aak-oauth-trust.yml` under `trusted_client_ids:`. Rotate the consent if the client isn't recognised.
rules.title: Third-party OAuth client granted broad Workspace scopes

rules.description: Tool description contains invisible Unicode characters (zero-width joiners, RTL overrides, invisible separators) that could hide malicious instructions.
rules.limitations: Reads description strings only: a tool's own, its input schema's, each parameter's, and the `toolDescriptions` map, in the `mcpServers` (or VS Code `servers`) object of an MCP config file; what a server returns from `tools/list` at run time is not read. The same invisible characters in a tool `name` or `title`, or in a parameter's `default`, `enum` or `examples`, are not read. Characters that render blank without being format or combining marks, such as the Braille blank (U+2800) and the Hangul filler (U+3164), are not matched either.
rules.remediation: Remove invisible characters from tool descriptions.
rules.title: Invisible Unicode characters in tool description

rules.description: Tool description contains prompt injection patterns such as 'ignore previous instructions', 'system:', or role-switching directives.
rules.limitations: Matches a fixed list of phrases: `ignore previous`, `system:`, `you are`, `forget`, `new instructions`, `override`, `admin mode`, `<hidden>` and `<system>`. The same instruction in other words is not matched, for example `ignore all previous instructions` (a word sits between the two), `disregard the instructions above`, or an `<IMPORTANT>` block that tells the model to keep a step from the user.
rules.remediation: Delete or reword the phrase quoted in the finding so the description only says what the tool does. The rule matches `ignore previous`, `system:`, `you are`, `forget`, `new instructions`, `override`, `admin mode`, `<hidden>` and `<system>` (case-insensitive), so a harmless phrase such as 'the files you are allowed to read' needs rewording too.
rules.title: Prompt injection patterns in tool description

rules.description: Tool description references other tools by name, potentially triggering chain calls (e.g., 'before using this tool, first call X').
rules.limitations: Matches five phrases: `before calling`, `first call`, `after using`, `then use` and `invoke`. A description that sends the model to another tool in other words is not matched, for example `run get_credentials afterwards`, `send the page text to send_email` or `call read_secrets with the same arguments`; a tool name on its own is never matched.
rules.remediation: Tool descriptions should be self-contained and not reference other tools.
rules.title: Cross-tool reference in tool description

rules.description: Tool description contains base64, hex, or URL-encoded content that could hide malicious instructions.
rules.limitations: Matches a single run of 40 or more base64 characters, three or more `\xNN` escapes, or three or more `%NN` in a row. The same payload split into shorter pieces with spaces, written as `&#NN;` entities or `\uNNNN` escapes, or run through ROT13, is not matched.
rules.remediation: Replace the encoded text with plain text, or delete it. The rule matches 40 or more consecutive letters, digits, `+` or `/` (base64-like), three or more consecutive `\xNN` escapes, and three or more consecutive `%NN` sequences in a description.
rules.title: Encoded content in tool description

rules.description: Tool description exceeds 500 characters, which increases the surface area for hidden instructions.
rules.limitations: The 500-character limit is applied to each description string on its own. A tool whose description and parameter descriptions each stay under it is not reported, however much instruction text they add up to.
rules.remediation: Keep tool descriptions concise and under 500 characters.
rules.title: Excessive tool description length

rules.description: Tool description contains URLs or file paths that could direct the agent to access external resources.
rules.limitations: Matches `http://` and `https://` URLs, a `/` followed by three or more path characters, `~/`, and an upper-case drive letter such as `C:\`. A bare hostname or address (`collector.example.com:8443`), a lower-case drive letter (`c:\Users\...`) and a `%USERPROFILE%\...` path are not matched.
rules.remediation: Remove URLs and file paths from tool descriptions.
rules.title: URL or file path in tool description

rules.description: A hook bridge, gateway or guard cuts a candidate command, URL or path to a fixed length "for matching", evaluates its deny / block patterns against the cut copy, and hands the full untruncated value to whatever executes it. Everything past the cut point is invisible to the policy and visible to the executor, so a caller simply positions the dangerous part after the bound and the hard-deny list never sees it. The disclosed instance is CVE-2026-73614 (Network-AI ClaudeHookBridge < 5.15.1, CVSS 8.8): the target string is truncated to 500 characters before `denyPatterns` are evaluated while Claude Code executes the full Bash command field. That package is not pinnable — it resolves on neither npm nor PyPI and its GitHub repository 404s — so this rule is written against the shape rather than the vendor, and applies to any policy code with the same asymmetry. It fires only when the untruncated source is still referenced elsewhere in the file, which is what separates a policy/executor split from ordinary display truncation.
rules.limitations: Looks for `x = y.slice(0, 500)` (or `substring`, `substr`) or `x = y[:500]` with a numeric literal of two or more digits, tested within 400 characters of a name that contains `deny` or `block` and then ends in Pattern, List, Rule, Match, Regex or `s` (`denyPatterns`, `bashDenyList`, `DENY_PATTERNS`, `blockedList`) or contains forbidden, disallow, blacklist or hard-deny, while `y` is still used untruncated. A bound held in a constant (`slice(0, MAX_MATCH_LEN)`), a slice written `y[0:500]` and a list named `deniedPatterns` are not matched.
rules.remediation: Evaluate the policy against exactly the value the executor receives. If a length bound is needed to cap matching cost, reject over-long input outright rather than matching a prefix of it — a truncated match is a decision made on data that is not what runs. Where the check and the execution live in different components, pass one canonical value between them instead of letting each derive its own.
rules.title: Deny policy evaluated on a truncated copy of the value the executor receives

rules.description: A pricing function (set_price / quote / bid / list_price / negotiate / price_item / compute_price) calls an LLM with a templated `model=` argument and is not gated by `@aak.parity.check` (or equivalent). Anthropic's 2026-04-26 Project Deal experiment found Opus sellers earned $2.68/item more than Haiku sellers despite identical buyer ratings (4.06 vs 4.05). This is OWASP LLM09 (overreliance / economic harm) — without per-tier parity assertions, deploying multiple model tiers behind the same pricing surface produces silent revenue / cost drift across customer cohorts.
rules.limitations: Python only, and only for a function whose whole name is `set_price`, `quote`, `bid`, `list_price`, `negotiate`, `price_item` or `compute_price`: `get_quote` is not checked. The LLM call must be one of the listed SDK spellings with a `model=` keyword (`litellm.acompletion`, or a model passed inside `**params`, is not matched), and the module must import `stripe`, `shopify`, `medusa` or `commercetools` or have `pricing/` or `commerce/` in its path; a file under `marketplace/` is out of scope. A Python file over 512 KB is not read.
rules.remediation: Wrap pricing functions with `@aak.parity.check(dimensions=['model'], metric='price', max_drift_pct=1.5)` and run `aak parity report` in CI. The decorator records every invocation's (model, price) tuple and raises `ParityDriftError` if any per-tier mean drifts more than the configured threshold from the overall mean.
rules.title: Cross-tier LLM pricing without parity check (Project Deal class)

rules.description: A function pulls a title-like field from a GitHub event source (`pull_request.title`, `pull_request.head.ref`, `issue.title`, or env vars wired to the same) and feeds it into an LLM client call (`anthropic.messages.create`, `openai.chat.completions.create`, `genai.GenerativeModel.generate_content`, `langchain.*.invoke`) without an HTML-escape, allow-list, or hash on the title. Aonan Guan's 2026-04-25 Comment-and-Control disclosure (CVSS 9.4) showed an attacker-controlled PR title injects instructions the agent executes with its own credentials — credential theft demonstrated against Claude Code Security Review, Gemini CLI Action, and GitHub Copilot Agent.
rules.limitations: Needs, in one Python function (or one TS/JS file), a title source, an LLM client call and no sanitiser. An event read is a source when it reads the PR or issue title or the PR head ref as an attribute, a subscript or a `.get()` (`pull_request.title`, `event["pull_request"]["title"]`, `event.get("issue", {}).get("title")`), so `pull_request.body` is not a source, and neither is TypeScript's optional chaining (`payload.pull_request?.title`) or a `.get()` whose default is itself a call (`event.get("pull_request", dict())`); a sink is one of the listed spellings (`client.messages.create`, `openai.chat.completions.create`), so `client.chat.completions.create` is not one. Any `json.dumps(`, `re.escape(`, `hashlib.*(` or `html.escape(` in the function counts as a sanitiser, including a `json.dumps` that only builds the prompt. A file over 512 KB is not read.
rules.remediation: Wrap the title in `html.escape` (or `markupsafe.escape`), or validate against a strict allow-list, or hash it before interpolating into the prompt. For TS/JS, use the equivalent. For shell-style agents, prefer `shlex.quote`. The fix is structural — never interpolate untrusted GitHub event content into an LLM prompt.
rules.title: PR/issue title flows into LLM client without sanitiser

rules.description: A routine configuration declares tool permissions wider than what the same user has in interactive Claude Code. A routine running non-interactively at 3am with admin-level tools is an excessive-agency risk (OWASP ASI02 over-privileged tool access, with no human to notice).
rules.limitations: Reads the `permissions` (or `tools`) list of a file in `.claude/routines/` and reports an entry only when it is exactly `fs:*`, `shell:exec`, `network:*`, `credentials:*`, `env:*` or `*:*`. Other spellings of the same breadth (`shell:*`, `Bash(*)`, `*`) are not reported, and neither is a `permissions` block written as a mapping (`allow: [...]`). A routine file over 1 MB is not read.
rules.remediation: Mirror routine permissions from the interactive grant. Require re-prompt for elevation.
rules.title: Routine grants broader permissions than interactive path

rules.description: A routine's cron expression, HTTP webhook URL, or GitHub event filter is built from a user-controlled value. Schedule injection can repurpose the routine at off-hours without review.
rules.limitations: Reads the first of `schedule`, `cron` or `trigger` that is set, and only when it is a string containing `${`, `{{` or `%{`, so a static `schedule` hides an interpolated `trigger` beside it. A `trigger` written as a mapping (`type: webhook` with a `url` holding `${TENANT}`), a webhook URL in a key of its own, and `$(...)` substitution are not read. A routine file over 1 MB is not read.
rules.remediation: Treat schedule expressions as static constants; never build them from runtime state.
rules.title: Routine schedule interpolates unsanitized input

rules.description: A routine runs tool calls but writes no run-log, making post-hoc audit impossible. An attacker with edit access to the routine file can run anything and delete the evidence.
rules.limitations: Looks for the key `audit_log`, `audit`, `log` or `output_log` and not at its value, so `audit_log: false` or an empty `log:` counts as an audit trail. A routine file over 1 MB is not read.
rules.remediation: Route every routine's output (and tool-call trace) to an append-only log the routine cannot modify.
rules.title: Routine executes without audit trail

rules.description: A tool's definition (name, description, or input schema) has changed since it was last pinned. This could indicate a rug pull attack. The Deadbugz campaign (September 2026) is the shape this is for: an MCP server shipped two innocuous tools, behaved for exactly three tool calls, then rewrote the metadata it returned into instructions to hunt SSH keys, AWS credentials, shell history and kubeconfig. Metadata that only turns hostile at runtime defeats review by construction, because every check you run before approving the server passes. A pin taken at approval and re-verified afterwards is what closes that window, and this rule is that comparison.
rules.limitations: Compares the tool definitions written in the MCP config files with `.agent-audit-kit/tool-pins.json`; what a server returns from `tools/list` at run time is never compared. The hash covers a tool's name, description and `inputSchema` only, so a change to its `annotations` (for example flipping `readOnlyHint`), its `title`, or a schema kept under `parameters` is not a change here. A pin file over 1 MB, or one nested past 500 levels, is not read: the scan reports it as incomplete and compares nothing.
rules.remediation: Review the changes. If legitimate, re-pin with 'agent-audit-kit pin'. If suspicious, remove the server. Re-run 'agent-audit-kit verify' on a schedule rather than only at install time: a campaign that waits N calls before mutating is invisible to a one-off check at approval.
rules.title: Tool definition changed since last pin

rules.description: A new tool was added to an MCP server since the last pin. New tools should be reviewed before approval. The Deadbugz campaign (September 2026) added capability after approval rather than at install time, which is why the comparison has to run again after the server is already trusted.
rules.limitations: Counts only tools declared in a server's `tools` array in a config file. A server added with just a `command`, whose tools arrive at run time through `tools/list`, adds no pinned tool, and neither does a tool listed under `toolDescriptions`, so a new server or a new tool of those shapes is not reported here. A pin file over 1 MB, or one nested past 500 levels, is not read: the scan reports it as incomplete and compares nothing.
rules.remediation: Review the new tool's definition and permissions. If it is expected, run `agent-audit-kit pin .` to record it in `.agent-audit-kit/tool-pins.json`; if not, delete its entry from the server's `tools` list. Pinning records every current tool, so deal with any other drift findings first.
rules.title: New tool added since last pin

rules.description: A previously pinned tool was removed from an MCP server. This could indicate covering tracks after an attack.
rules.limitations: Counts only tools declared in a server's `tools` array in a config file, because nothing else is pinned.
