A JavaScript file is skipped as a bundle when its name holds `.min.`, or when it is over 10,000 characters and its median non-blank line (the longer of the middle two, for an even number) is over 500 characters long or most of it is lines over 5,000 characters in which `(` and `;` make up at least 1%. So a one-line bundle of 10,000 characters or fewer is read, and a hand-written file most of whose text is one long line of inlined data with `;` in it, such as a stylesheet or an SVG, is skipped, and its findings with it.
rules.remediation: Validate and sanitize file paths. Use os.path.realpath() and verify against allowed directories.
rules.title: Tool parameter flows to file open

rules.description: A @tool function parameter is passed to requests.get/post or urllib, enabling SSRF attacks.
rules.limitations: Only functions decorated `@tool`, `@mcp.tool`, `@server.tool`, `@langchain.tools.tool`, `@crewai.tool` or `@autogen.tool`, and a low-level `@<server>.call_tool()` handler, are analysed, so a FastMCP instance under another name (`@app.tool()`) is skipped. Reports `requests.get/post/put/delete`, `httpx.get/post` and `urllib.request.urlopen`, written that way or imported under another name (`from urllib.request import urlopen`), when the URL is not a literal and an argument is a parameter, an item read from one or, in a `call_tool` handler, a local holding one at most two assignments away. A local in a `@tool` function (`target = url`) is not followed. An imported name the file also binds some other way anywhere, a method included (`def get(self, key)` in an unrelated class silences `from requests import get`), and every name in a file with a star import, is matched by its spelling only. A client instance (`await client.get(url)` on an `httpx.AsyncClient`) and `requests.request("GET", url)` are not matched.
rules.remediation: Validate the URL against a host allowlist and refuse internal and private addresses, then give the validated value to the request through a call or a new name, such as `requests.get(checked_url(url))`. The rule fires whenever a tool parameter is passed to the HTTP call under its own name, validated or not.
rules.title: Tool parameter flows to HTTP request

rules.description: In Python, a @tool function parameter, or an item read from one, is passed as the whole query to cursor.execute(), connection.execute() or session.execute(), so the caller chooses the SQL that runs. The TypeScript and JavaScript arm reports a template literal with an interpolation passed to .query(), .execute() or .raw(), a string literal concatenated into .query() or .execute(), and Prisma's $queryRawUnsafe and $executeRawUnsafe; the Rust arm, a sql!, query! or query_as! macro given a format! string or a concatenation that starts with a bare name (`sql!(base + id)`).
rules.limitations: Only functions decorated `@tool`, `@mcp.tool`, `@server.tool`, `@langchain.tools.tool`, `@crewai.tool` or `@autogen.tool`, and a low-level `@<server>.call_tool()` handler, are analysed, so a FastMCP instance under another name (`@app.tool()`) is skipped. The Python arm reports `cursor.execute`, `connection.execute` and `session.execute` only when a parameter, or an item read from one, is the whole argument, that is, a caller-supplied query, and not when a local holds it, even in a `call_tool` handler (`sql = arguments["sql"]`, then `cursor.execute(sql)`). A query built from the parameter, whether by an f-string (`cursor.execute(f"SELECT * FROM notes WHERE title = '{title}'")`), `.format()`, `%` or `+`, the usual shape of SQL injection, is not reported, and neither is the same call on a variable under another name (`conn.execute(query)`). The TypeScript and JavaScript arm reads the template literal or the concatenation on the call's own line, so a query built into a variable first (`db.query(sql)`), or one whose `${` falls on a later line, is not reported. It reads a `.js`, `.jsx`, `.mjs` or `.cjs` file only when the file imports the SDK's server modules, registers a tool or handles `CallToolRequestSchema`. A JavaScript file is skipped as a bundle when its name holds `.min.`, or when it is over 10,000 characters and its median non-blank line (the longer of the middle two, for an even number) is over 500 characters long or most of it is lines over 5,000 characters in which `(` and `;` make up at least 1%. So a one-line bundle of 10,000 characters or fewer is read, and a hand-written file most of whose text is one long line of inlined data with `;` in it, such as a stylesheet or an SVG, is skipped, and its findings with it.
rules.remediation: Use parameterized queries. Never use f-strings or .format() for SQL.
rules.title: Tool parameter flows to SQL query

rules.description: A @tool function parameter is passed to pickle.loads(), yaml.load(), or similar deserialization functions.
rules.limitations: Only functions decorated `@tool`, `@mcp.tool`, `@server.tool`, `@langchain.tools.tool`, `@crewai.tool` or `@autogen.tool`, and a low-level `@<server>.call_tool()` handler, are analysed, so a FastMCP instance under another name (`@app.tool()`) is skipped. Reports `pickle.load/loads`, `yaml.load/unsafe_load` and `marshal.loads` when the argument is a parameter, an item read from one or, in a `call_tool` handler, a local holding one at most two assignments away. A local in a `@tool` function (`data = blob`) is not followed. Other loaders that can run code from the data are not sinks: `torch.load`, `joblib.load` and `dill.loads` are not reported.
rules.remediation: Use safe deserialization (yaml.safe_load, json.loads) instead of unsafe alternatives.
rules.title: Tool parameter flows to deserialization

rules.description: A @tool function has no type hints or input validation on its parameters.
rules.limitations: Only functions decorated `@tool`, `@mcp.tool`, `@server.tool`, `@langchain.tools.tool`, `@crewai.tool` or `@autogen.tool` are analysed, so a FastMCP instance under another name (`@app.tool()`) is skipped. A tool counts as typed once any one parameter carries an annotation: `def search(query: str, limit, path)` is not reported, however many parameters have none.
rules.remediation: Add type hints and input validation to all tool function parameters.
rules.title: Tool function missing input validation

rules.description: A @tool function calls sinks of three or more of the categories behind AAK-TAINT-001 to -006 (shell, eval/exec, file access, HTTP, SQL, unsafe deserialization), whether or not a parameter reaches them, which indicates overly broad permissions. A pathlib.Path read only for a part of its name (Path(p).name) opens nothing and does not count as file access, so a tool calling subprocess.run, requests.post and Path(p).name reaches two.
rules.limitations: Only functions decorated `@tool`, `@mcp.tool`, `@server.tool`, `@langchain.tools.tool`, `@crewai.tool` or `@autogen.tool` are analysed, so a FastMCP instance under another name (`@app.tool()`) is skipped. Sink categories are counted only for calls made in the body of the decorated function, so a tool that reaches a shell, a file and the network through module-level helper functions it calls is not reported.
rules.remediation: Split the tool so that each function reaches at most two of the sink categories behind AAK-TAINT-001 to AAK-TAINT-006 (shell, `eval`/`exec`, file access, HTTP, SQL, unsafe deserialization). The rule fires at three.
rules.title: Tool function with excessive dangerous sinks

rules.description: A task read endpoint returns task state based on the task ID alone. Any caller that guesses or enumerates a task ID gets another user's data (CWE-639).
rules.limitations: Reads only files that contain a task marker: `task_id`, a `class` whose name contains Task, `Task` or `task` directly followed by Manager, Store, Queue, Runner, Primitive or SEP-1686 (`TaskStore`), or `/tasks/{`, `/tasks/:` or `/tasks/<`. In them it looks for a Python `def` named get_task, read_task, task_read, get_by_id or findTask and clears it when one of the whole words owner, requesting_user, current_user, authenticated_user, principal, tenant_id or caller_id (any case; `owner_id` does not count) appears in the next 1200 characters. A TypeScript or JavaScript handler (`async function getTask`) and a file with no task marker are not matched, and the word `owner` counts even when the function only returns it.
rules.remediation: Verify the caller is the task owner (or has an explicit grant) before returning task state.
rules.title: MCP task read endpoint lacks per-task authorization

rules.description: A task record retains API keys / OAuth tokens after the task reaches a terminal state (completed/failed/cancelled). Long-lived credentials in persistent state are an obvious exfil target.
rules.limitations: Looks for `self.credential`, `self.credentials`, `self.api_key`, `self.token`, `self.secret` or `self.password` assigned in a file with a task class and one of the words completed, failed, cancelled, done, finished or terminal (matched inside longer words too), and clears the finding when any `self.<name> = None`, `del self.<name>`, `clear_secret(`, `zeroize(` or `zero_ize(` appears in the file. A different attribute name (`self.access_token`) is not matched, and a clearing statement that never runs on the terminal transition, such as a `reset()` nothing calls, still counts.
rules.remediation: Zeroize credential fields when the task transitions to a terminal state. Keep only what a post-mortem actually needs.
rules.title: MCP tasks persist credentials past completion

rules.description: A task record has no expiration and no cancellation endpoint. Orphaned tasks accumulate forever, including their inputs.
rules.limitations: Fires on a task class or store with no `ttl`, `expires_at`, `expiry` or `deadline` assignment and no `def cancel_*`, `abort_*` or `terminate_*` in the file. Any such assignment counts, whatever it applies to: a `ttl=60` on an unrelated cache call clears it.
rules.remediation: Set a TTL on every task; expose a cancellation endpoint that zeroizes inputs and credentials.
rules.title: MCP task has no TTL or cancellation path

rules.description: The MCP Tasks primitive (SEP-2663) exposes a task-creation path (`tasks/create`, `create_task`, `enqueue`, `submit`) with no per-caller quota, max-in-flight, or concurrency bound. Unbounded task creation lets a caller flood the server with long-running tasks and exhaust memory / worker capacity — a task-flood denial of service. This is distinct from a missing TTL / cancellation path (AAK-TASKS-003): a server may expire and cancel tasks yet still accept unlimited concurrent creation.
rules.limitations: Fires when a file with a task class has a creation path (`tasks/create`; a `def` named create_task, add_task, spawn_task, start_task, `enqueue*` or `submit*`; or a call to `create_task(`, `enqueueTask(`, `submitTask(` or `addTask(`) and none of max_tasks, maxTasks, task_limit, quota, max_concurren*, concurrency_limit, max_in_flight, max_pending, rate_limit*, ratelimit, backpressure, Semaphore or BoundedSemaphore, in any case, with `_` or `-` between words optional (`maxInFlight`, `max-tasks`). `createTask(` is not recognised as a creation path, and a quota word in a comment counts as a bound.
rules.remediation: Bound task creation: a per-caller quota and a max-in-flight / concurrency cap (e.g. a bounded semaphore or a queue depth limit), and reject or back-pressure creation once the bound is reached.
rules.title: MCP Tasks creation has no quota / concurrency bound (task-flood DoS)

rules.description: Source code wires a social-platform reply sink (`tiktok_api.reply`, `instagrapi.direct.send`, `tweepy.API.update_status`, `discord.Message.reply`, etc.) to a user-content source (`comments.fetch`, webhook payload `text` field, media comments) without an `aak.review.human_in_loop()` / `human_in_the_loop()` / `require_approval()` gate. Jiacheng Zhong's BlackHat Asia 2026 (2026-04-24) talk demonstrates hijacks in this class — attacker posts a crafted comment that the agent's own reply loop turns into a tool call, reflecting attacker text back to the platform's audience. OWASP LLM08 (Excessive Agency).
rules.limitations: Reads .py files only. It fires on one that calls `tiktok_api.reply(`, `tiktok.comment.reply(`, `instagrapi.direct.send(`, `instagrapi.<x>.comment_reply(`, `tweepy.API().update_status(`, `tweepy.Client().create_tweet(`, `discord.Message.reply(` or `discord.Channel.send(` and also reads `event["comment"]`, `comments.fetch(`, `webhook.payload["text"]`, `tiktok_api.comments`, `instagrapi.<x>.comments` or `media.comments`, with none of `aak.review.human_in_loop(`, `human_in_the_loop(`, `require_approval(` or `needs_review(`. A reply sent through an instance (`await message.reply(text)`) is not matched. A Python file over 512 KB is not read.
rules.remediation: Place every social-platform write call behind a human-review gate. AAK ships an `aak.review.human_in_loop(text, comment=...)` helper that defaults closed and requires explicit approval (CLI, webhook, or workflow). For high-volume agents, route generated replies to a moderation queue instead of the platform sink directly.
rules.title: Social-agent auto-reply without human-in-loop gate

rules.description: An agent project exposes both a sensitive source tool (filesystem read, secrets read, database query) and an external sink tool (HTTP POST, email send, git push) without an explicit `.aak-toxic-flow-trust.yml` allow-list entry. Even if each tool is individually safe, the LLM can chain them — the canonical exfil pattern is `read_file -> http.post`. Suppress with an allow-list when the pairing is a documented product feature.
rules.limitations: Off unless `AAK_TOXIC_FLOW=1` is in the environment. It reads the server names and `args` strings of `.mcp.json`, `.cursor/mcp.json`, `.vscode/mcp.json`, `.amazonq/mcp.json` and `mcp.json` at the scan root, and the names of Python functions decorated `@tool`, `@mcp.tool` or `@server.tool` with no arguments, and matches each against the names in `toxic_flow_pairs.yml`. A server is judged by its name and arguments, not by the tools it lists at run time, so `@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem`, whose read tool is `read_text_file`, is no source. A decorator with arguments (`@tool("read_file")`, `@mcp.tool(name=...)`), a TypeScript `server.tool(...)` and a skill under `.claude/skills/` declare no tool. A Python file over 512 KB, or an MCP config or trust file over 1 MB, is not read.
rules.remediation: Add the source/sink pair to `.aak-toxic-flow-trust.yml` with a `justification:` field, scope the source tool to a directory the sink cannot reach, or remove one side of the pair. The finding's evidence names the families and the tools on each side.
rules.title: Toxic flow: sensitive source paired with external sink

rules.description: An MCP server URL uses a cleartext scheme, exposing all traffic including credentials to interception. **Applies to: `http://` and `ws://`.** A `ws://` handshake is an unencrypted HTTP upgrade, so it is the same defect and not a milder one -- the handshake headers and every frame after them are on the wire in clear. **Does not apply to: `https://`, `wss://` (encrypted), or `stdio` (no URL, no network hop).** Loopback URLs (`localhost`, `127.0.0.0/8`, `::1`, `0.0.0.0`) are excluded on either scheme, since the traffic does not leave the host.
rules.limitations: Reads the `url` field of each server under `mcpServers`, or `servers` in VS Code's `.vscode/mcp.json`, and flags `http://` and `ws://` unless the host is loopback (localhost, 127.0.0.0/8, ::1) or 0.0.0.0. The scheme is read as a client reads it, so ` http://host` and `http:/host` are cleartext too. A URL that Node, requests and Rust's `url` crate read differently from curl, httpx and urlsplit, which keep a backslash inside the authority, is judged by the less safe of the two readings. A cleartext URL passed as an argument to a bridge command (`npx mcp-remote http://...`) is not a `url` field and is not read.
rules.remediation: Use `https://` for remote HTTP/SSE/Streamable-HTTP servers and `wss://` for remote WebSocket servers.
rules.title: MCP server uses a cleartext transport (http:// or ws://)

rules.description: TLS certificate validation is disabled via NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0 or similar, enabling MITM attacks. **Applies to: every TLS-bearing transport -- `https://`, `wss://`, and TLS-wrapped SSE/Streamable HTTP.** The setting is read from the server's `env` block rather than its URL, so it is transport-independent: it disables peer verification for whatever the process connects to. **Does not apply to: `stdio`** (no TLS peer to verify).
rules.limitations: Matches `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0` and any `SSL_CERT_FILE` in the `env` block of a server under `mcpServers`, or `servers` in VS Code's `.vscode/mcp.json`. Other switches that turn certificate checking off, such as `NPM_CONFIG_STRICT_SSL=false`, are not read.
rules.remediation: Delete `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED` (when it is `0`) and `SSL_CERT_FILE` from the server's `env`, the two settings this rule matches. If the server must trust a private CA, add it through the runtime's extra-CA setting (for Node, `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS`) instead of switching verification off or replacing the CA bundle.
rules.title: TLS certificate validation disabled

rules.description: An MCP server uses deprecated Server-Sent Events (SSE) transport instead of Streamable HTTP. **Applies to: `sse` only** -- matched from an explicit `"type": "sse"` or `"transport": "sse"` (any case), or a `/sse` path in the URL. **Does not apply to: `stdio`, `http`/`streamable-http`, or `ws`/`wss`.** WebSocket is a different transport, not a deprecated one: it is outside this rule rather than silently passing it.
rules.limitations: Fires once per server, on a `type` or `transport` key set to `sse` in any case, or else on a `url` that contains `/sse` as a whole word (`/sse_events` does not count). A server that names SSE only under another key, such as `transportType`, at a URL without a whole-word `/sse` is not matched.
rules.remediation: Migrate to Streamable HTTP transport (MCP spec 2025-03-26+).
rules.title: Deprecated SSE transport in use

rules.description: A session token or API key is passed as a URL query parameter, risking exposure in logs and referrer headers. **Applies to: every URL-bearing transport -- `http`/`https`, `ws`/`wss`, and SSE/Streamable HTTP**, including loopback URLs, since the exposure is the URL being written down (proxy logs, shell history, referrer headers) rather than the hop being observed. A WebSocket handshake URL is logged by the same intermediaries as any other request line. **Does not apply to: `stdio`** (no URL).
rules.limitations: Looks for `?` or `&` followed by token, key, api_key, apikey, secret, auth, access_token or session_token and `=` in the server `url`. Other parameter names (`?api-key=`, `?jwt=`) and a credential carried in the URL path (`/s/abc123/mcp`) are not matched.
rules.remediation: Pass tokens in HTTP headers instead of URL query parameters.
rules.title: Session token in URL query parameter

rules.description: Auto-approves ALL MCP servers in .mcp.json without user consent. A compromised repo can ship arbitrary MCP servers that execute immediately.
rules.limitations: Reads `.claude/settings.json` and `.claude/settings.local.json` at the root of the scanned directory. The same flag in the settings file of a subdirectory (`packages/web/.claude/settings.json`) is not read.
rules.remediation: Set to false. Use enabledMcpjsonServers to whitelist specific servers by name.
rules.title: enableAllProjectMcpServers is true

rules.description: Redirects all API traffic (including API keys) to attacker-controlled endpoint BEFORE trust prompt displays. This is the exact attack vector of CVE-2026-21852.
rules.limitations: Parses `env.ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` in `.claude/settings.json` and `.claude/settings.local.json` at the root of the scanned directory and accepts it when the host is `anthropic.com` or a subdomain of it, whatever the scheme, so a cleartext `http://api.anthropic.com/v1` passes. A URL that Node, requests and Rust's `url` crate read differently from curl, httpx and urlsplit, which keep a backslash inside the authority, is judged by the less safe of the two readings, so `https://api.anthropic.com\@evil.example/v1`, Anthropic to Claude Code and evil.example to the httpx-based Python SDK, is reported. The same override in the settings file of a subdirectory (`packages/web/.claude/settings.json`) is not read.
rules.remediation: NEVER override ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL in project settings. Only set in user-level or system environment.
rules.title: ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL overridden in project settings

rules.description: Permission allow patterns use wildcards (*, **) or broad tool names. This bypasses the permission system, allowing unchecked tool execution.
rules.limitations: Matches only the exact strings `*` (or any run of asterisks), `mcp__*`, `Bash(*)`, `Edit(**)`, `Read(**)` and `Write(**)` in `permissions.allow`. A bare tool name (`Bash`) or a prefix grant (`Bash(sudo:*)`) is not matched.
rules.remediation: Use narrowest possible permission patterns. Specify exact tool names and path constraints.
rules.title: Wildcard or overly broad permission allows

rules.description: Settings file has permission allows but empty or missing deny rules. Defense-in-depth requires explicit deny rules for sensitive operations.
rules.limitations: Fires when `permissions.allow` has entries and `permissions.deny` is empty or missing. Any non-empty deny list clears it, whatever it denies: `Read(./docs/notes.md)` beside `Bash(curl:*)` passes.
rules.remediation: Add deny rules for: file system operations outside project, network tools, credential-accessing tools.
rules.title: No deny rules defined

rules.description: An environment variable matching *_BASE_URL, *_API_URL, or *_ENDPOINT is set in project settings. This can redirect authenticated traffic to attacker-controlled servers.
rules.limitations: Matches `env` names that end in `_BASE_URL`, `_API_URL` or `_ENDPOINT`. Other spellings that point a client at another server (`OPENAI_API_BASE`, `LLM_GATEWAY_URL`) are not matched.
rules.remediation: Set API URLs only in user-level configuration or system environment variables.
rules.title: Custom API base URL for any provider

rules.description: Project settings have permission allows that could shadow user-level deny rules. Misconfigurations can create a false sense of security.
rules.limitations: Counts an allow entry only when its text contains Bash, Edit, Write, Read or `mcp__`. Allowing `WebFetch` or `Task` with no deny list is not reported.
rules.remediation: Audit that project allows don't re-enable operations the user intended to block.
rules.title: Project settings may override user deny rules

rules.description: The project's settings file has no `enabledMcpjsonServers` key while a root `.mcp.json` declares servers, so which of them Claude Code may start is decided by whoever answers the prompt rather than by the project.
rules.limitations: Fires only when a settings file at the root of the scanned directory sits beside a root `.mcp.json`. A package directory that carries its own `.claude/settings.json` and `.mcp.json` (`packages/web/`) is not looked at. A present `enabledMcpjsonServers` key is the allowlist, an empty list included: `[]` approves no server, the strictest allowlist there is, and it is what `aak fix` writes, so the fix clears the finding. Through 0.6.24 an empty list fired too, and `aak fix` reported a change that cleared nothing. It reads the key, not the value: a list of names is the allowlist whether or not `.mcp.json` declares them.
rules.remediation: Configure enabledMcpjsonServers with explicit server names.
rules.title: No MCP server allowlist configured

rules.description: A project settings file (`.claude/settings.json`, or a committed `.claude/settings.local.json`) sets a proxy (`HTTPS_PROXY`, `HTTP_PROXY`, `ALL_PROXY`), a certificate authority to trust (`NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS`, `SSL_CERT_FILE`, `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE`) or `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0` in its `env`. Claude Code's settings reference says `env` applies "for every session and for the subprocesses Claude Code starts from it", from project settings once the folder is trusted and at once in `-p` mode, and its network configuration page says each proxy and CA variable "can also be configured in settings.json" and that a terminal session reads them "from every settings scope". A repository that sets them sends the API traffic of everyone who opens it, credentials included, through a proxy it names, or has their session and the servers and commands it starts trust a certificate authority it chose, which together let it read and change that traffic. Where Claude Desktop manages the connection it ignores these variables in a repository's own settings files, "so a checked-out repository can't redirect the TLS or proxy path of a session"; a terminal session has no such guard.
rules.limitations: Reads the `env` object of `.claude/settings.json` and `.claude/settings.local.json` at the root of the scanned directory, whether or not the second is committed (AAK does not ask git), and reports `HTTPS_PROXY`, `HTTP_PROXY` and `ALL_PROXY` in any case, `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS`, `SSL_CERT_FILE` and `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE` as written, each with a value that is not blank, and `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED` set to `0`. The user's own `~/.claude/settings.json`, where the docs put these variables, is not reported, even with `--include-user-config`. `NO_PROXY`, `CLAUDE_CODE_CERT_STORE`, the mTLS client certificate variables, other switches with the same effect on the programs a session starts (`CURL_CA_BUNDLE`, `GIT_SSL_NO_VERIFY`), and a settings file in a subdirectory (`packages/web/.claude/settings.json`) are not read.
rules.remediation: Remove the proxy and certificate variables from the project settings' `env`. Set them in `~/.claude/settings.json`, managed settings or your shell, where Claude Code's network configuration docs put them, so each user chooses their own network path. Never commit `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0`.
rules.title: Proxy or certificate-authority override in project settings
